item.content:encoded:
This year's World Series will have a tough act to follow. Not only was the 2025 World Series between the Los Angeles Dodgers and Toronto Blue Jays the first seven-game affair since 2019, but it featured an 18-inning game and then a Game 7 that might have been the greatest baseball game ever played.
The good news is we're guaranteed that a long-starved fanbase will get to celebrate in 2026. The Milwaukee Brewers, coming off their impressive and dynamic four-game sweep of the Dodgers in the NLCS, are in the Fall Classic for the first time since 1982 and seek the first championship in franchise history, looking to put an exclamation point on their season after leading the majors with 103 wins.
The Tampa Bay Rays were a 1998 expansion franchise and reached the World Series in 2008 and 2020 (the shortened season during the COVID-19 pandemic) but are seeking their first title as well. Young power hitter Junior Caminero and unheralded staff ace Drew Rasmussen lead the way as the Rays look to finally cash in after making the playoffs six times in the past eight seasons.
The Brewers and Rays led their respective leagues in wins, always a bonus for those who want the best teams in the World Series. Of course, a lot of attention will be given to the small-market aspect of the matchup, as the cloud of the lockout looms in the offseason.
Let's rank all the World Series since 2000 to see where Brewers-Rays fits in. This ranking is based on hype, the quality of the teams and their star power heading into the World Series. It's not a ranking of the quality of the World Series itself, although we're going to include a grade on that for each matchup. Let's get to it.
The Yankees were back in the World Series for the sixth time in eight years, and the Marlins had rebuilt after their fire sale following their World Series title in 1997. Trust me when I say that nobody wanted the Yankees in the World Series yet again. And the Marlins were merely a 91-win wild-card team. Most notably, however, both teams had spoiled the ultimate World Series by knocking off the Cubs and Red Sox -- before either team had overcome its curse -- in Game 7s in the LCS.
Actual World Series: C. The Marlins won Game 4 in 12 innings, when Yankees manager Joe Torre inexplicably failed to use reliever Mariano Rivera, and then 23-year-old Josh Beckett tossed a five-hit shutout in Game 6.
In an all-wild-card series, the fifth-seeded Rangers had won 90 games and the sixth-seeded Diamondbacks won only 84, making this the lowest combined win total in World Series history (for full seasons). The Rangers were going for their first World Series title, so there was that, and there were some fun hitters -- Corey Seager, the red-hot Adolis Garcia (who had just driven in 15 runs in the ALCS) and Corbin Carroll -- but it was a soft matchup on paper.
Actual World Series: D-. The series turned on Seager's tying two-run homer off Paul Sewald in the bottom of the ninth of Game 1, which Garcia then won with a home run in the 11th. There wasn't a single lead change after that, and three of those games were blowouts.
This was the Cardinals team that got hot in September and clinched a wild-card spot on the final day of the season when the Braves blew a lead in the ninth inning and lost in extra innings. St. Louis certainly had star power with the likes of Albert Pujols, Lance Berkman and Matt Holliday but had won a World Series fairly recently (2006), and the Rangers had just been there the year before.
Actual World Series: A. The first two games were one-run games, including the Rangers pulling out a victory with two runs in the ninth. In Game 3, Pujols blasted a record-tying three home runs. Game 6 was the David Freese Game -- perhaps the single most exciting baseball game ever played. Game 7 was a bit of an anticlimactic 6-2 Cardinals win.
The second-lowest combined win total in World Series history featured two wild-card teams that won fewer than 90 games. The Royals were at least a good story -- in the playoffs for the first time since winning the World Series in 1985 -- and had gone 8-0 in the AL playoffs, including an epic win over the A's in the wild-card game. The Giants, however, had just won the World Series in 2010 and 2012, and this team didn't seem nearly as good as those two.
Actual World Series: B-. Five of the games were blowouts, but it did at least go seven. It'll be remembered for Madison Bumgarner's historic performance: a shutout in Game 5 (the last complete game shutout in World Series history) and then five scoreless innings of relief in Game 7, getting Salvador Perez to pop out with the tying run on third to end it.
The Red Sox were only three years removed from breaking the Curse of the Bambino in 2004, so although they were still a star-laden team with David Ortiz, Manny Ramirez and scrappy rookie Dustin Pedroia, they were no longer as interesting. The Rockies were a fun story, winning 14 of their final 15 games, including beating the Padres in a tiebreaker, just to win a wild-card spot. Then they went 7-0 in the NL playoffs and had won 21 of 22 entering the World Series.
Actual World Series: F.A dud. Two of the games were one-run games, but this goes down as one of the least memorable World Series of all time, with a forgettable four-game sweep.
The Tigers were the story of the season. They had lost 119 games three years before and 91 just the previous year. With rookie starter Justin Verlander winning 17 games, they led the AL Central most of the season -- only to lose their final five games and squeak into the playoffs as a wild-card team. The Cardinals won a weak NL Central with only 83 wins -- although they at least had Pujols at his absolute peak (.331/.431/.671, 49 home runs). Both teams hadn't won a World Series in a couple of decades: 1982 for the Cardinals, 1984 for the Tigers. Plus, it did feature two of the original 16 franchises.
Actual World Series: F. The Cardinals won one game in the bottom of the eighth, but it was otherwise a blur of nothing, most characterized by several fielding miscues by Tigers pitchers. David Eckstein won MVP honors without hitting a home run and while driving in only four runs.
The Braves were back in the World Series for the first time since 1999 -- they had made 12 playoff appearances in the intervening years without making it to the Fall Classic. Still, this was the weakest of the Atlanta playoff teams of recent vintage, winning only 88 games and missing Ronald Acuña Jr. for the playoffs. The Astros, meanwhile, were back in the World Series for the third time in five years -- but the first time since the 2017 sign-stealing scandal had broken in November 2019. Let's just say not everyone wanted them there.
Actual World Series: D. This was a weird World Series. The Braves ended up going with two bullpen games (who remembers that Dylan Lee and Tucker Davidson started?) after Charlie Morton broke a leg in Game 1. Astros starters kept getting knocked out early (the only starter to go more than five innings for either team was Max Fried in the finale). Four of the games were blowouts.
The Giants were back after winning in 2010, and the Tigers were back for the first time since 2006, featuring Triple Crown winner Miguel Cabrera and a strong 1-2 punch in the rotation with Verlander and Max Scherzer. This was also the last World Series with that season's MVP winners until Aaron Judge and Shohei Ohtani in 2024, with Cabrera and Buster Posey.
Actual World Series: D-. A boring sweep. Pablo Sandoval did hit three home runs in Game 1, but there were two shutouts and chilly weather in Detroit made the final two games unbearable.
This one did feature the two best teams from the regular season (both won 97 games), the last time before this year that we had that happen in a full season. It was also a classic original-16 matchup, although we had seen this in 2004 -- plus, both teams had won recently (2007 for Boston, 2011 for St. Louis). These were veteran teams, with Ortiz leading the Red Sox and the Cardinals featuring four .300 hitters, plus Carlos Beltran, who hit .296 and led the team in home runs.
Actual World Series: C+. Ortiz was absolutely locked in, hitting .688/.760/1.188 with two home runs and eight walks. The Cardinals were so scared of him by Game 6 that they intentionally walked him three times -- with two of those helping lead to rallies and a 6-1 Red Sox victory in the final game.
This one could be No. 25 -- it was during the pandemic, after all, and it was played at a neutral site in a half-empty stadium for social distancing reasons. But it was a great matchup between the teams with the best records in each league, albeit over the shortened 60-game season. You had Mookie Betts and Clayton Kershaw and Randy Arozarena in the midst of one of the best postseasons ever, plus the small-market Rays trying to beat the big-market Dodgers.
Actual World Series: C+. Because teams were allowed an expanded roster of 28 players, it was a parade of relievers -- but there were some fun games, including a bonkers ending to Game 4 and then Rays manager Kevin Cash's controversial decision to remove Blake Snell in Game 6, which backfired in a big way.
Maybe this should rate higher. After all, at the time, the White Sox were trying to break a World Series drought going back to 1917 and the Astros, born in 1962, had never won. But the White Sox's drought never had the same nationwide interest as the ones for the Cubs or Red Sox (fair or not) and these weren't particularly interesting teams. The White Sox were very good -- they won 99 games -- but lacked star power, with Paul Konerko their biggest name (Frank Thomas was on the team that year but played only 34 games and was injured for the playoffs). The Astros had Yankees transplants Roger Clemens and Andy Pettitte, but their two longtime stars, Jeff Bagwell and Craig Biggio, were at the end of their careers (Bagwell, in his final season, was relegated to DH and pinch-hitting duties).
Actual World Series: C. It's hard to give a sweep a decent grade, but all four games were exciting, including Scott Podsednik's walk-off home run in Game 2 (after not hitting a home run all season) and Geoff Blum's go-ahead home run in the 14th inning to win Game 3.
The Phillies were back in the World Series for the first time since 1993 -- and hadn't won since 1980. They featured a powerful offense with Chase Utley, Ryan Howard, Jimmy Rollins and Pat Burrell. The Rays were maybe the unlikeliest World Series team ever: In their 10 previous years of existence, they had not only never had a winning season but had lost at least 90 games in each one. They won 97 games that year behind rookie Evan Longoria and power-hitting first baseman Carlos Peña, with speedsters Carl Crawford and B.J. Upton in the outfield.
Actual World Series: D+. Three games were decided by one run, but it was a pretty uneventful World Series. The lasting memory is the cold and rain in Philly that forced the midgame postponement of Game 5, the only time that has happened in World Series history. The game was suspended in the sixth inning and resumed two days later.
A Subway Series -- the first since the Yankees and Brooklyn Dodgers met in 1956 -- was certainly fun for the Big Apple, but it was less fun for the rest of the country (it drew the worst TV ratings at the time). The Yankees were going for a third straight World Series and had officially become the Evil Empire by that point. To make it even worse, they weren't even that good that season, winning only 87 games. The Mets were back in the World Series for the first time since 1986. There was certainly plenty of star power all around with the likes of Derek Jeter, Roger Clemens and Mike Piazza.
Actual World Series: C+. It was a tight-fought five-game series with all games decided by two runs or fewer. The turning point was the bottom of the ninth of Game 1, when the Yankees tied it off Armando Benitez and went on to win in 12 innings. Game 2 featured the infamous Clemens-Piazza bat-throwing incident, and the Yankees won the clincher with two runs in the ninth off a tired Al Leiter.
I know, the Astros ... again. Boo. But this was an absolute powerhouse of a team with 106 wins and stars such asYordan Alvarez (1.019 OPS) and Verlander (18-4, 1.75 ERA), plus the old standbys Jose Altuve and Alex Bregman. The Phillies, meanwhile, snuck in as a wild-card team for their first playoff trip since 2011 but were an immensely entertaining team with Bryce Harper, Kyle Schwarber& Co., as well as a passionate fanbase cheering them on.
Actual World Series: C. The Phillies won 6-5 in Game 1 on J.T. Realmuto's home run in the 10th inning. They took a 2-1 series lead, but then their bats died. Astros pitchers tossed a combined no-hitter to even the series, and Houston won the final two games 3-2 and 4-1, with Alvarez's three-run blast in Game 6 the deciding blow.
The Brewers' drought is the big narrative here as they try to finally cash in after their past decade of success, but we're still getting the 103-win Brewers facing the 98-win Rays, the best combined win total in the World Series since the Astros and Dodgers in 2017. (Not to mention we get a first-time winner no matter the outcome.) The Brewers aren't your conventional powerhouse team -- relying on speed, defense, timely hitting and a dominant bullpen -- but they do have one of the biggest stars of the 2026 season in Jacob Misiorowski, plus a rising star in young Jackson Chourio. The Rays might lack big names, although Junior Caminero is just the second player with two 40-homer seasons by age 22, and like the Brewers, they're trying to finally win it all after years of success.
Actual World Series: To be determined.
The Royals proved their 2014 World Series appearance was no fluke, winning 95 games with a better team that included trade deadline additions Ben Zobrist and Johnny Cueto. The Mets won the NL East behind a young, powerful rotation that featured Matt Harvey, Noah Syndergaard and Jacob deGrom. It was a fun matchup of teams trying to avoid lengthy title droughts -- 30 years for the Royals, 29 for the Mets.
Actual World Series: C+. It went only five games, but the Royals won the opener in 14 innings, won Game 5 with a three-run eighth inning and then won the clincher in 12 innings -- after Mets manager Terry Collins' ill-fated decision to leave in Harvey to start the ninth with a 2-0 lead.
This was a super entertaining showdown at the time. The Giants had yet to win a World Series in San Francisco and featured Tim Lincecum ("The Freak," for his small stature and overpowering stuff) and two rookies named Posey and Bumgarner. The Rangers had never won a championship and featured AL MVP Josh Hamilton and veteran DH Vladimir Guerrero. Both teams had pulled off upsets in the LCS, with the Giants beating the Phillies and the Rangers beating the Yankees.
Actual World Series: D. Meh. The Giants won the opener in a blowout as the Rangers made four errors and then tossed shutouts in Games 2 (behind Matt Cain) and 4 (behind Bumgarner). You can test Giants fans by asking them who won World Series MVP honors that year. Answer: Edgar Renteria (he hit .412 with two home runs and six RBIs).
Remember, this happened before the sign-stealing scandal changed how we view this era of the Astros. They had won 107 games behind the pitching duo of Verlander and Gerrit Cole and four players who mashed 30-plus home runs (which didn't even include Alvarez, a rookie that year). The Nationals were a wild-card team that had overcome a 19-31 season start to win 93 games and featured a starting pitching trio of Scherzer, Stephen Strasburg and Patrick Corbin (and 20-year-old sensation Juan Soto, who hit 34 home runs).
Actual World Series: B-. It went seven games -- the road team would win all seven -- although five of the games weren't close. The best game was the last one: The Nationals went ahead 3-2 in the seventh inning on Anthony Rendon's home run and then Howie Kendrick's go-ahead home run just inside the right-field foul pole.
This matchup began with a lot of hype: Shohei Ohtani, coming off his all-time game in the NLCS in which he hit three home runs and struck out 10 batters as the starting pitcher, against Vladimir Guerrero Jr., who had hit .442 with six home runs through the first two rounds of the playoffs. The Dodgers were looking to become the first team with back-to-back titles since the 2000 Yankees and the first NL team since the 1976 Reds. The Blue Jays were back in the World Series for the first time since Joe Carter walked off the Phillies in 1993. Dodgers manager Dave Roberts stirred things up after the NLCS when he said during the postgame celebration, "Let's get four more wins and really ruin baseball" -- a reference to the criticism of the Dodgers' high payroll.
Actual World Series: A+. The Dodgers won Game 3 in 18 innings on Freddie Freeman's walk-off home run, which followed an unlikely four-inning relief performance from Will Klein, the last guy on the Dodgers' staff. The Dodgers went back to Toronto trailing 3-2 but won Game 6 behind Yoshinobu Yamamoto and a crazy game-ending double play.
Game 7 featured two future Hall of Famers starting in Ohtani and Max Scherzer, more on-the-edge-of-your-seat plays than any game in World Series history, Miguel Rojas' unlikely home run in the ninth to tie it, as well as Will Smith's go-ahead one in the 11th -- and finally, Yamamoto pitching in relief to close out the game by inducing a double play with two runners on to win it for the Dodgers. It wasn't quite the greatest World Series overall, but two all-time games made it a classic.
The Angels, who joined the majors in 1961, were making their first World Series appearance, while the Giants, in the Bay Area since 1958, were trying to win their first title since moving from New York. You had Barry Bonds at the height of his unstoppable powers -- and trying to erase his own postseason demons -- while the Angels had a loaded lineup (Troy Glaus, Tim Salmon, Garret Anderson), the Rally Monkey and those deafening ThunderStix (let us pray they never return).
Actual World Series: A. Bonds was a beast, hitting .471/.700/1.294 (yes, that's a 1.994 OPS), but it wasn't enough. This series featured four one-run games, including a wild 11-10 contest and the classic Game 6, when the Angels rallied late from a 5-0 deficit to win 6-5. Game 7 was a drab 4-1 contest (Bonds went a harmless 1-for-3).
The Yankees had missed the playoffs in 2008 for the first time since 1993, so they went out and signed free agents CC Sabathia, Mark Teixeira and A.J. Burnett to add to an already stacked roster that included Jeter, Alex Rodriguez, Robinson Cano, Hideki Matsui, Jorge Posada and Johnny Damon. Whoa. Yes, they were still the Evil Empire. The Phillies, trying to defend their title, had traded for Cliff Lee and then signed Pedro Martinez in July to bolster their rotation.
Actual World Series: C. It could have been a classic battle, but there were no one-run games and Game 6 -- Martinez's final start of his career -- was over early. The crucial contest was Game 4, when the Yankees scored three runs in the ninth off Phillies closer Brad Lidge to win 7-4.
This one presented conflicting emotions. The Yankees were going for an unthinkable fourth straight title, but in the wake of 9/11, there was a "Win it for New York" angle that the Yankees had never encountered. The Diamondbacks, meanwhile, had the big, bad duo of Randy Johnson and Curt Schilling. When asked on the eve of the World Series about the Yankees' mystique and aura, Schilling provided one of the great quips in World Series history: "Mystique and Aura? Those are dancers at a nightclub." The Diamondbacks were not going to be intimidated.
Actual World Series: A+. Four one-run games, including three of the most memorable World Series moments ever: Jeter's Mr. November home run to win Game 4, Scott Brosius' walk-off home run to win Game 5 and then Luis Gonzalez's bloop single to beat the invincible Mariano Rivera in Game 7.
Two of baseball's most historic franchises had never met in a World Series, creating the classic showdown with games in Fenway Park and Dodger Stadium. It doesn't get any better than that. The Red Sox were a 108-win powerhouse -- with AL MVP Mookie Betts leading the way, backed up by J.D. Martinez, who hit .330 with 43 home runs that season. Chris Sale and David Price headlined the rotation. The Dodgers actually had a bit of a down year with 92 wins, but they also weren't lacking in big names, with Manny Machado (a trade deadline acquisition), Yasiel Puig, Matt Kemp, Cody Bellinger and Justin Turner, with Kershaw and rookie Walker Buehler on the pitching side.
Actual World Series: C-. A letdown. The first two games in Fenway were cold and windy. Game 3 was an 18-inning affair -- the longest in World Series history -- but was more of a slog than a game to remember. Game 4 was the best of the series as the Red Sox rallied with nine runs over the final three innings to win 9-6.
This series had it all: dominant teams (both won over 100 games), long World Series title droughts (never for the Astros, 1988 for the Dodgers) and superstars galore (Altuve, Verlander, Carlos Correa, Kershaw, Seager, Bellinger, Yu Darvish). We didn't know at the time that both franchises were just kicking off 100-win dynasties -- let alone what the Astros were doing behind the scenes -- but the anticipation level was off the charts for the first matchup of 100-win teams in the World Series since 1970.
Actual World Series: A-. Game 1, with a start-time temperature of 103 degrees at Dodger Stadium, was a Kershaw 11-strikeout gem. The Astros tied Game 2 in the ninth on Marwin Gonzalez's home run off Kenley Jansen (1.32 ERA that season), both teams scored twice in the 10th, the Astros scored twice in the 11th on George Springer's home run and held on for a 7-6 win. Game 4 featured a five-run rally in the ninth by the Dodgers to win. Game 5 was completely bananas, with the Astros finally winning 13-12 in 10 innings. Game 7 was a letdown though, as the Astros won a 5-1 snoozer in which they scored five runs off Darvish in the first two innings.
As mentioned, what's not to like? Aside from Ohtani and Judge each playing in their first World Series and trying to put a final stamp on their legacy-defining seasons, we hadJuan Soto and Mookie Betts, a suddenly rejuvenated Giancarlo Stanton and a hobbled Freddie Freeman (only raising the drama if he hit well), Gerrit Cole and Yoshinobu Yamamoto. Aside from the history between the clubs, we had both clubs needing to rewrite their recent history: The Yankees, back in the World Series for the first time since 2009, and the Dodgers trying to add a more legitimate championship to the one they won in the COVID-shortened season.
Actual World Series:C+. The Judge-Ohtani showdown was a flop, as Judge hit .222 with one home run and Ohtani hit .105 without a home run or RBI. The series also went just five games, with the Dodgers winning the first three. The series did produce two forever moments, however: Freeman's walk-off, Kirk Gibson-esque grand slam in Game 1 and the Yankees' fifth-inning defensive meltdown in Game 5.
The Red Sox were coming off their never-done-before comeback from down 3-0 to beat the Yankees in the ALCS -- and still had to beat a 105-win Cardinals team that featured Pujols (.331, 46 home runs), Jim Edmonds (.301, 42 home runs) and Scott Rolen (.314, 34 home runs), plus in-season pickup Larry Walker, who had an OPS over 1.000 that year. The Red Sox had their own ridiculous lineup with Ortiz (.301, 41 home runs), Ramirez (.308, 43 home runs) and Damon (.304, 20 home runs) plus a rotation with Schilling and Martinez. It seems inevitable now that Boston was going to win, but that wasn't the case at the time, so the buildup was intense.
Actual World Series: D. Blah. I mean, Red Sox fans will rightfully call it the best World Series ever, but after a sloppy 11-9 Game 1 played in a drizzle at Fenway (the Red Sox won despite committing four errors), the Cardinals never led again.
The Cubs had not only not won since 1908, but they hadn't even been in a World Series since 1945. The Guardians, meanwhile, had the second-longest drought of the original 16 teams, without a title since 1948. That was enough right there to build up the anticipation, but this also rates high because it was two good teams -- Chicago won 104 games while Cleveland won 94. Cubs third baseman Kris Bryant won MVP honors that year and Cleveland was led by 18-game winner Corey Kluber (who would start three times) and young rising stars Francisco Lindor and Jose Ramirez.
Actual World Series: B. The first six games weren't anything too special, but Game 7 was one of the greatest in World Series history. Cleveland tied it on Rajai Davis' three-run homer in the bottom of the eighth, the Cubs scored twice in the 10th -- following a stress-filled rain delay -- and escaped with an 8-7, curse-ending win when Cleveland had to bat little-used Michael Martinez with its season on the line.

Estados Unidos/Un viaje a la Serie Mundial está de por medio en el Juego 6 mientras los Rays trasladan la SCLA de vuelta al Tropicana Field.
Tras su victoria por 3-1 sobre los Guardianes en el Juego 5, los Rays lucen ahora como la mejor versión de sí mismos, jugando una defensa hermética detrás de un pitcheo élite y haciendo lo justo en el plato para que todo funcione.
Estos dos equipos son muy similares, comenzando desde la base de cómo adquieren y desarrollan talento, hasta cómo manejan los partidos jornada tras jornada, por eso no esperen palizas. Sin embargo, la estrella de los Rays, el cubano Yandy Díaz, tiene una predicción llena de confianza tras conectar cinco hits en los últimos dos encuentros en Cleveland.
Si los Guardianes pretenden robarse dos partidos ante los Rays en St. Petersburg y concretar otra sorpresa, tal como lo hicieron en la SDLA contra los Medias Blancas, necesitarán silenciar a Díaz, al mexicano Jonathan Aranda y al dominicano Junior Caminero, el 'Big Three' que encabeza la alineación del conjunto de Tampa Bay que están dando señales de vida. Sin embargo, todo comienza detrás de Díaz, el exjugador de los Guardianes que ha sido una de las caras de los Rays desde el 2019.
Te puede interesar: MLB resutado | Rays vencen a Guardianes y toman ventaja 3-2 en la Serie de Campeonato de la Liga Americana
Lanzadores abridores
Guardianes: Shawn Armstrong, LD
Datos clave: Ha lanzado cuatro entradas en blanco a lo largo de tres presentaciones en la SCLA, incluyendo un inning sin carreras concedidas como opener en el Juego 4.
Armstrong tendrá su segundo turno como opener en esta serie. A partir de ahí, Cleveland volverá a armar un juego del bullpen después de que la corta apertura de Parker Messick en el Juego 4 causara que Armstrong, Tim Herrin, Erik Sabrowski, Hunter Gaddis y Cade Smith cubrieran siete entradas. Debido a que Cleveland está en una situación de ganar o irse a casa, se contempla que gran parte de esos muchachos estén disponibles el lunes. Pero Slade Cecconi, Joey Cantillo y Tanner Bibee podrían tener que desempeñar un rol importante también, después de que ninguno lanzara en el Juego 5. Williams no es una alternativa para lanzar con corto descanso, según dijo Vogt tras el Juego 5.
Rays: Freddy Peralta, LD
Datos clave: Marca de 6-0 con efectividad de 0.79 en nueve presentaciones (ocho aperturas) desde el 26 de agosto.
Peralta está de vuelta lanzando a su mayor nivel, como lo indican los números anteriores. No estuvo del todo eficaz saliendo del bullpen para conseguir un par de outs en el Juego 4 el sábado, pero ha estado dominante en ocho aperturas desde finales de agosto. Y ha estado excelente en cinco aperturas en el parque de los Rays durante ese trecho, recetando 26 ponches contra ocho bases por bolas otorgadas, registrando efectividad de 0.99.
"Lo que ha hecho en casa, increíble. Pensé que volvió a ser un atleta con nosotros y no tan robótico", señaló el abridor Drew Rasmussen. "La verdad le dio la libertad de ser exactamente quien pensábamos que sería cuando lo conseguimos en la Fecha Límite de Cambios".
La presentación en relevo de Peralta ocurrió en lugar de su sesión del bullpen programada entre aperturas, por lo que eso no debería afectar ninguno de los planes de Tampa Bay en el futuro.

Datos adicionales
- El exjardinero central de los Rays, B.J. Upton, realizará el primer pitcheo ceremonial antes del Juego 6. Upton desempeñó un rol bastante importante en el camino de Tampa Bay al título de la Liga Americana en el 2008, sacudiendo siete jonrones en la postemporada, incluyendo cuatro en el triunfo de los Rays en siete juegos en la SCLA sobre Boston.
- La racha de Ramírez de 17 juegos embasándose en postemporada es la más larga en la historia de la franquicia de Cleveland.
- El pitcheo de Cleveland recetó seis ponches en el Juego 5, para llevar su total de postemporada a 120 a lo largo de sus 10 encuentros. Los 120 ponches son la tercera mayor cantidad para cualquier equipo de las Mayores en sus primeros 10 partidos de una postemporada, solo por debajo de los 123 de los Nacionales del 2019 y los 122 de los Astros del 2022.
- Fijándonos hacia adelante, la Serie Mundial del 2026 presentará un enfrentamiento inédito por séptima vez en las últimas ocho campañas (desde el 2019). En ese transcurso, la única Serie Mundial entre equipos que se habían enfrentado en un Clásico de Otoño previo fue en el 2024 (Dodgers vs. Yankees).
- Un choque de Serie Mundial entre Tampa Bay y Milwaukee sería el primero en un Clásico de Otoño entre equipos buscando su primer campeonato desde 1980 (Phillies vs. Reales).

The Minnesota Twins have spent another October watching the postseason from home and the biggest question is why. The Twins have missed the playoffs in five of the past six seasons and while many are rightfully upset about the team’s payroll slashing, there are also several fundamental mistakes that have prevented them from being successful.
Those mistakes will be front and center during this year’s World Series. The Milwaukee Brewers punched their ticket to the Fall Classic after completing a sweep over the Los Angeles Dodgers on Thursday night and they will face either the Tampa Bay Rays or Cleveland Guardians in what will be a showdown between small-market teams.
While this year’s matchup could create a loophole for the Pohlad family to avoid dropping a large amount of money to improve the team, it also reflects poorly on their decisions that have kept them from competing over the past few years.
The Brewers, Rays and Guardians are showing the Twins how to build a winner
As you may have guessed, the Brewers, Guardians and Rays are not among MLB’s biggest spenders. According to Cot’s Baseball Contracts, the Brewers’ year-end salary ranked 23rd at $99.3 million and defeated the Dodgers’ No. 1 roster at $366.0 million. The American League finalists were also budget-conscious as the Rays ranked 20th with a year-end payroll of $103.1 million and the Guardians ranked 25th at $91.0 million.
All three of the remaining teams had a lower year-end payroll than the Twins, who ranked 17th with a figure of $123.9 million and while many, including owner and chairman Tom Pohlad, believe that adding to that number could lead to a championship, the other three teams show what they have done wrong.
The first is maximizing the value of players on the roster. The Rays, Guardians and Brewers have traded players before they get to free agency to add to their organization and it’s paid off in a big way. The Brewers most notably did this in a February 2024 trade featuring Corbin Burnes that brought back left-hander DL Hall and infielder Joey Ortiz.
The Rays also have done this with their trade of Triple-A right-hander Tobias Myers, who was traded to Cleveland as he was eligible for the Rule 5 Draft in 2021, and brought back star third baseman Junior Caminero in return. While the Guardians whiffed on Myers, they made other shrewd deals that netted them Craig Yoho, Patrick Bailey, Foster Griffin and Kyle Manzardo.
These trades are a double-edged sword as they usually involve popular players. But it brings back pieces that ensure a larger championship window. That leaves player development as the final phase of the three contenders and each team has a homegrown star to lean on such as Jose Ramirez, Jacob Misiorowski or Caminero.
The Twins’ biggest problems go beyond their payroll
Turning the attention back to the Twins, it’s easy to see where they have come up short. This year’s trade deadline was one opportunity to shift the narrative. But instead of trading players that could bring back a big return such as Ryan Jeffers and Joe Ryan, the Twins went the opposite direction, adding A.J. Minter, Jeff Hoffman and Dean Kremer.
Even when they tried to trade Trevor Larnach to the Houston Astros before owner Jim Crane vetoed it, they were seeking 29-year-old Bryan Abreu, a pitcher who posted his highest ERA (3.73) and lowest WAR (1.0) since his rookie season in 2021.
The other key issue is the Twins’ player development. While top prospects such as Royce Lewis and Matt Wallner thrive initially when reaching the major leagues, those players have hit a wall when pitchers adjust to them. The problem can be traced back to Miguel Sano’s downfall in the early 2020s and can still be seen in a group of post-hype hitters that haven’t lived up to their prospect status.
This leaves the Twins in a tricky spot this offseason. After failing to trade Jeffers at the deadline, there’s a good chance he’ll leave in free agency. Ryan has a year of team control remaining, but trading him now could get a pair of MLB-ready players in return. Several top prospects including Walker Jenkins, Emmanuel Rodriguez and Kaelen Culpepper made their debuts this season, but the key will be to make sure they don’t regress entering their first full season in the bigs.
Of course, fans may cheer for a salary floor to hold the Pohlads accountable for what happens to the Twins next. But the Rays, Guardians and Brewers show that paying top dollar may not be necessary to build a contender and Minnesota would be wise to follow their blueprint.

When the Brewers finished off the Dodgers on Thursday night, their World Series opponent was the last thing on anyone’s mind. An MLB official closed the postgame press conference by telling manager Pat Murphy and NLCS MVP Jake Bauers, “We’ll see you in Milwaukee at the World Series.”
Murphy’s reply said everything: “When’s that start?”
Next Friday, Oct. 23, at American Family Field, where Milwaukee holds home-field advantage thanks to its franchise-record 103 wins. The Guardians took a 2-1 ALCS lead over the Rays into Friday night's scheduled Game 4 at Progressive Field. Milwaukee, meanwhile, will have a full week to rest, which leaves plenty of time to watch and wonder.
Here’s a guide to each potential matchup. You decide which one you’d rather see.
If the regular season is a guide ...
It doesn’t tell us much. The Brewers went 2-1 against both teams.
Milwaukee won the first two games against Cleveland on June 16-17 before rookie left-hander Parker Messick struck out nine over six innings in the finale. Cleveland was without José Ramírez, Angel Martínez and Chase DeLauter. All three are back.
When the Brewers hit
Milwaukee’s lineup is built on pressure. The Brewers ranked in the top five in doubles, runs, hits, walks, batting average and on-base percentage.
That approach might get more of a test against Tampa Bay. The Rays issued the fewest walks in the Majors (409) and ranked second in defensive runs saved (87). Drawing walks and finding holes gets tougher against that combination. And their top starters have carried it into October: Drew Rasmussen has a 1.29 ERA through two postseason starts, while Peralta has allowed one earned run in 10 2/3 innings, including six shutout innings in Game 2 of the ALCS.
Cleveland offers a different challenge. Gavin Williams has been a monster, striking out 33 over 16 2/3 innings this postseason. The Guardians have a 2.54 ERA this October, slightly better than Tampa Bay’s 2.72. But Cleveland issued 530 regular-season walks to the Rays’ 409, giving Milwaukee more reason to believe its patient approach can create traffic.
When the other side hits
The regular-season numbers favor facing Cleveland. The Guardians had the lowest OPS (.696) and fewest runs (678) of any postseason team. Tampa Bay offered a more complete attack, with Junior Caminero’s 42 homers anchoring a lineup that tied for fifth in on-base percentage (.326).
October has told a different story. Through Thursday, Cleveland was averaging 4.25 runs per game with a .685 OPS, compared with Tampa Bay’s 3.00 runs and .563 OPS. The Guardians haven’t suddenly become an offensive powerhouse, but they’ve been more productive than the Rays, whose lineup managed just three hits in Game 3 of the ALCS.
The larger sample still points toward Cleveland as the preferable opponent. The way these teams are hitting right now makes that a tougher call.
The bullpens
Neither ninth inning looks inviting. Tampa Bay’s Bryan Baker has saved all four Rays wins this postseason without allowing a hit in four innings. Ian Seymour has been a strong bridge, allowing one earned run in 6 1/3 innings.
Cleveland counters with Cade Smith, who has allowed two hits and one run while striking out 13 in nine innings this October. Hunter Gaddis has added six scoreless innings across seven appearances. Both teams have arms capable of shortening games.
The Brewers have made a habit of coming back this postseason, and their bats have shown they can pick at a bullpen late. Against either opponent, getting a lead before the closer enters would make life easier.
What about the intangibles?
The Guardians’ championship drought dates to 1948. The Rays, like the Brewers, have never won a World Series.
The Rays mirror Milwaukee in many ways. Brewers president of baseball operations Matt Arnold worked in Tampa Bay’s front office alongside current Rays GM Erik Neander. Add Peralta facing his former team, and the storyline writes itself.
Cleveland manager Stephen Vogt played for Milwaukee and interviewed for the job that went to Murphy three years ago. And a Cleveland-Milwaukee World Series comes with a built-in movie reference: Major League, filmed in Milwaukee with Bob Uecker’s Harry Doyle calling Cleveland's improbable run.
The verdict
Give the Guardians a slight edge as Milwaukee’s preferred opponent, though their October bats have made that a tougher sell. The Rays were the more complete team over six months. Cleveland has spent the past two weeks making those six months feel a little less relevant.
The Brewers? They just sent the back-to-back champs home. They’ll let the AL sort this out. Somebody remind Murph what time Friday’s game starts.

item.content:encoded:
CLEVELAND -- It’s a new day in the ALCS, as the Rays and Guardians have shifted their matchup back to Cleveland tied up at 1-1.
The Rays' 3-1 win in Game 2 shifted this series back into focus after the Guardians pulled off a 7-3 come-from-behind win in the opener. We’ve seen each team’s best, and as these pitching staffs get stretched even thinner as the series wears on, they’ll need to lean on the identities they’ve built in 2026.
“It’s going to be a challenging place to play,” said Rays manager Kevin Cash. “We played there not too long ago in the postseason. That's as good an atmosphere as you're going to see. They've got a great fan base that's going to be behind their team. I'd like to think we can carry our momentum into there and just play good baseball for Game 3.”
Step back a few feet for a wider view, and this Guardians team has still won four of its past five games. The club ran into a Game 2 buzzsaw named Freddy Peralta, whose fastball was nearly unhittable, but Cleveland is still in an excellent spot after stealing Game 1.
“We feel great. Obviously we would have loved to have taken [Game 2],” Guardians manager Stephen Vogt said. “That would have been really big. And we had our position and our opportunities to do that. But going home 1-1, to go have three games in front of our fans in Cleveland, we feel really good about that. And we're excited to get it going.”
The pitching matchup has the potential to lean in the Guardians’ favor, too, with Gavin Williams starting on regular rest, fresh off a dominant outing against the White Sox to clinch the ALDS. For the Rays, Griffin Jax has been officially named the starter, and while he spent the majority of the season working in a true starter’s role, he pitched two innings of relief against the Yankees in Game 3 of the ALDS, throwing just 32 pitches.
This series is still waiting for its first show-stopping moment, too, with all eyes on José Ramírez for the Guardians and Junior Caminero for the Rays. Ramírez's series has been up-and-down so far, from a solid Game 1 to a crucial error that opened the door in Game 2, while Caminero is still searching for his first career postseason home run.
There’s history on the line here, too, for whichever team advances to represent the American League in the World Series. The Rays haven’t won the World Series since entering the league in 1998 and have only reached the big stage twice (2008, 2020). The Guardians, on the other hand, still carry the weight of the longest World Series drought in the big leagues at 77 seasons, stretching all the way back to 1948.
When is the game and how can I watch it?
First pitch for Game 3 of the Rays-Guardians American League Championship Series is scheduled for 1 p.m. ET on Thursday at Progressive Field. Due to inclement weather in the forecast, the original start time of 6 p.m. was moved up. The game will be broadcast on TBS and HBO Max. 
Spanish-language game broadcasts will be available on UniMas for the ALCS, and Spanish-language radio broadcasts will be available on Univision’s TUDN Radio.
Who are the starting pitchers?
Rays: Griffin Jax, RHP
Key Stats: 0.90 ERA over his past five appearances
Nick Martinez started ALDS Game 3 for the Rays, but they will turn to Jax this time after using him as a reliever against the Yankees, with Martinez likely in line to pitch Game 4 on Friday. Jax has been excellent since a rough return from the injured list on Sept. 2 after a bout of right elbow discomfort, permitting only two runs on 10 hits and four walks while striking out 19 in 20 innings over his last four regular-season starts and his Game 3 relief outing at Yankee Stadium. Jax is presumably prepared for Cleveland’s inclement weather, having pitched for Minnesota for most of his career, and he’s put up impressive numbers (including a 2.19 ERA, 0.89 WHIP and 20 strikeouts) in 13 relief appearances at Progressive Field.
Guardians: Gavin Williams, RHP
Key Stats: 1.54 ERA, 24 strikeouts in 11 2/3 innings in ALDS
The Guardians officially named Williams their Game 3 starter on Wednesday afternoon, setting the 27-year-old up for a start on normal rest following his heroic performance in the ALDS, when he made two starts and an emergency relief appearance against the White Sox. After he recorded the final three outs of Game 4, Williams came back on one day’s rest in Game 5 and tied a franchise postseason record in strikeouts (12) to help Cleveland beat Chicago, 2-0, to advance. Williams starting Game 3 also positions him to start a potential Game 7 of this series on Tuesday, on normal rest.
What are the starting lineups?
Rays: With Williams on the mound, the Rays are going with their standard lineup against right-handers, with the “Big Three” followed by their other left-handed hitters. They're staying with Jonny DeLuca, who’s started every postseason game so far, over Cedric Mullins in center field.
Guardians: Patrick Bailey is back behind the plate in Game 3. He and Williams have been a customary battery this season, and Bailey is swinging a hot bat this postseason. The Guards are sticking with the standard lineup they’ve had in this series.
How will the bullpens line up after the starter?
Guardians: Vogt will have a full bullpen at his disposal after the off-day, and will work getting the ball to closer Cade Smith. He and Hunter Gaddis did not appear in Game 2, after both pitched in each of the Guardians’ first six contests this postseason. Setup man Erik Sabrowski also did not pitch in Game 2 and will be working off two days’ rest.
Rays: The Rays should be in good shape after Wednesday’s off-day, although this will be the first time since the regular season that they’ve played three consecutive days in a row. Left-hander Ian Seymour has clearly established himself as a top setup option in front of closer Bryan Baker, and lefty Cam Booser has also been tasked with getting big outs against left-handed hitters. Right-hander Kevin Kelly and Tyler Wells are also setup options in front of Baker, who has recorded the save in each of Tampa Bay’s four wins this postseason.
Any injuries of note?
Guardians: None.
Rays: Caminero and DeLuca said they were fine after a nasty collision while chasing a foul ball in Game 1. Left-hander Shane McClanahan, who finished the regular season on the injured list due to left forearm tightness, was shut down for the rest of the postseason, Cash said on Sunday. Otherwise, nothing new.
Who is hot and who is not?
Guardians: Shawn Armstrong has allowed just one hit and struck out five batters in 5 1/3 scoreless innings over four postseason appearances. It’s been an impressive comeback after he missed two months with a left calf strain, before returning the final week of the regular season. DeLauter is hitting .346 (9-for-26) with just one strikeout in seven postseason games.
Rocchio is hitting .091 (2-for-22) in seven games.
Rays: Pretty much everyone who touched the mound for Tampa Bay in the ALDS and Game 2 of this series performed well, which is certainly promising for the team moving forward, even after some shaky bullpen work in Game 1. The Rays are starting to find some rhythm at the plate, too, with Caminero leading the way despite not yet having the big moment everyone’s expecting. Hicks drove in a couple runs in Game 2, and DeLuca had his second straight multihit game. Díaz is just 5-for-21 in the playoffs, and Mesa is only 3-for-18.
Anything else fans might want to know?
• Cleveland Cavaliers guard Donovan Mitchell will throw the ceremonial first pitch before Game 3.
• With his fifth-inning single in Game 2, Ramírez moved into second place in franchise history in postseason hits (49), breaking a tie with Kenny Lofton. Omar Vizquel (57) ranks first.
• Game 2 of the ALCS was Díaz’s 30th postseason game with the Rays, matching Evan Longoria for the most in franchise history. Game 3 should give Tampa Bay’s DH the club record.
• The Rays are 89-0 this year, including the regular season and postseason, when leading after eight innings. The last team to go a full year with a 1.000 winning percentage and at least 89 wins when leading after eight innings? The 2022 Mets, who went 90-0. The last team to do so in the AL was the 2002 Athletics (93-0).

Well, OK, Guardians fans know it. And even casual fans know by now that Ramírez is a dynamic player. The "underrated" label has long since stopped applying to this seven-time All-Star.
With Ramírez’s Guardians in an ALCS that continues with Game 3 on Thursday night at Progressive Field, it’s a good time to share some fun and fascinating elements of his story that many fans might not be aware of. Though the prevailing narrative at this moment is his rare defensive miscue that opened the doors to the Rays’ win in Game 2, Ramírez is the primary reason the Guardians are in the ALCS in the first place, and his talent and personality are worth celebrating.
Here are -- appropriately, for the man who wears No. 11 for Cleveland -- 11 things every baseball fan should know about José Ramírez.
1) He hates being called 'J-Ram'
Let’s get this one out of the way right away. “J-Ram” is anathema to Ramírez, who is far too dynamic for such a dull nickname anyway.
If you must use a folksy nickname, “Hosey” works. But in Cleveland, Ramírez doesn’t need a nickname or a last name. He’s simply “José” (and it sounds best when sung to the stadium anthem “Ole! Ole! Ole!”).
2) He’s put the Guardians on his back
It’s funny to think that, a little more than a week ago, people were questioning Ramírez’s October clutchness. He had an injury-riddled regular season and struggled through Game 2 of the ALDS against the White Sox, with the Guardians down 0-2.
Be it the stakes or the crowd riding him, something snapped in Game 3. From that point on, he went 5-for-12 with five runs scored, seven RBIs, two homers, a double and a triple over three games. In the Game 5 clincher at home, he somehow golfed a curveball virtually in the dirt for a career-defining home run, then followed it up with a three-hit night in Cleveland’s Game 1 win in the ALCS.
As teammate Chase DeLauter put it: "He's the G.O.A.T. … When he comes out and has that kind of fire, it lights all of us up.”
3) He’s a likely future Hall of Famer
The postseason was the one element lacking from Ramírez’s resumé prior to this fall, but his Cooperstown case is already shaping up nicely. He sits at 60.3 bWAR, just 8.6 shy of the average of third basemen in the Hall of Fame, with a seven-year peak bWAR (44.7) just below Brooks Robinson’s (45.8).
At age 34, he is just three regular-season home runs shy of joining Alex Rodriguez as the only third basemen, shortstops, or second basemen with at least 300 homers, 400 doubles, 300 steals, and 1,000 RBIs. He’s finished as an AL MVP finalist four times. Last year, Sarah Langs made the definitive case for him as the best player never to win the award.
4) He’s a throwback
The stats are nice, but it’s the way this compact, 5-foot-8 player gets to them that makes him so fun to watch.
It’s pure hustle -- dirty uniforms, flying helmets and natural instincts. His steals stem from situational intelligence rather than elite speed, while his range, fluidity, and elite pitch-reading allow him to play an above-average hot corner and avoid strikeouts despite modest raw bat speed and arm strength.
5) His baseball smarts are off the charts
In the ninth inning of ALCS Game 1, Ramírez broke for third and came around to score when Jo Adell rolled a grounder through the left side of the infield. Cameras caught Ramírez laughing as he crossed home plate. 
Why? After the game, his agent relayed that Ramírez had planned the whole play out: He knew that Kevin Kelly was going to throw a changeup. He knew that Adell was going to roll over on it and hit a grounder to the left side. By stealing, he pulled Rays third baseman Junior Caminero to the bag -- and opened a hole exactly where the ball ended up going.
Ramírez will venture away from the on-deck circle just to get a better view of a pitcher's release point, playing the game through anticipation rather than mere reaction. One of his greatest joys is putting pressure on opponents by drawing throws, taking secondary leads and creating openings for his teammates.
Surrounded by younger players on a budget-conscious roster, he constantly tries to impart these nuances, noting, "When these guys really focus and pay attention to the game, we score a lot of runs."
6) He has humble roots
Hailing from Baní in the Dominican Republic, Ramírez grew up playing baseball on a rocky dirt square, crossing the Río Baní from a rural home that lacked running water.
Financial limitations meant playing with a glove that was too tight and using water jug caps as baseballs in games of "Vitilla.” A major childhood lifeline came when former AL MVP Miguel Tejada held a local clinic distributing equipment and food. Ramírez rushed to the front of the line.
“I never forgot it,” he said.
7) He was only scouted by accident
Undersized and often the youngest player in his league, a 13-year-old Ramírez played in rough adult leagues watched over by gamblers, with a machete dangling behind home plate as a warning for poor performance.
Scouts weren't watching him; he was usually just an extra man at showcases. But in 2009, Cleveland scouting director John Mirabelli and scout Ramon Peña happened to catch him filling in for another player and ripping hits in bunches. Peña pounded the table for him, and Ramírez was signed for $50,000.
“He’s not the guy that came in with a lot of acclaim,” Guardians president of baseball operations Chris Antonetti said. “He wasn’t afforded a ton of extra opportunities because of an investment.”
8) He’s incredibly loyal
That modest $50,000 investment bought an extraordinary level of allegiance.
Ramírez faced a crossroads in 2022, when the Guardians were contemplating a trade before his final two control years. Ramírez wanted no part of leaving. He implored his agent to secure a deal that would keep him in Cleveland, prioritizing happiness and stability over free-agent riches.
“I’m happier with $150 million in Cleveland,” he told his agent, according to an ESPN report, “than $200 million somewhere else.”
Now signed through his age-39 season, he explains it simply: "Cleveland is everything to me. When nobody wanted to give me a chance, they gave me a chance."
9) His community work is not just lip service
Crediting his late grandmother, Santa Ramírez, with teaching him the value of sharing his success, José insisted on partnering with the Guardians on community impact projects. He funded the $2.7 million José Ramírez Field alongside Cleveland Guardians Charities, serving the Lincoln-West High School team and Cleveland's Nike RBI program on a street the city proudly named José Ramírez Way.
He has also helped expand MLB's Fun At-Bat program locally and teamed up to completely refurbish the rough field in Baní where he first learned to play, making it a safe and usable space for the next generation of ballplayers.
“The reality,” he said, “is that those kids in the D.R. have no alternative. That’s why I feel it’s really important to help.”
10) He respects the game
While his famous 2023 altercation with Tim Anderson spawned popular Cleveland T-shirts celebrating the "Down Goes Anderson" moment, Ramírez was actually mortified by it. He never wants to show up an opponent or be viewed as a troublemaker, emphasizing that his goal is always to give 100 percent and set an example.
At its core, Ramírez has said what he loves most about baseball is that it is "a disciplined way of learning how to respect each other."
11) He’s hilarious
Cutthroat on the field, Ramírez loves to keep people loose off it.
He’s worn a chain with a picture of himself. Wearing a chain. He’s worn a belt adorned with his image, too.
He’s joked that he’s “more beautiful” than Shohei Ohtani. He’s yelled to Freddie Freeman, “You’re one of the best hitters … after me.”
He trash talks teammates during games of Mario Kart or playfully smacks them in the back of the head when it’s time to pay attention. Once, when a teammate was smashing an iPad after a bad at-bat, Ramírez calmly told him, “Bro, settle down, that iPad can’t hit.” He’ll field another player’s position during batting practice and josh about how easy it is.
Ultimately, he’s a connector of people, keeping things fresh with deadpan humor that keeps people guessing.
Now you know José Ramírez. He might not be your favorite player yet. But hopefully you understand why he’s a favorite to so many.

The Cleveland Guardians wouldn't be heading into Game 2 of the ALCS with a 1-0 series lead over the Tampa Bay Rays if it weren't for the heroics that superstar Jose Ramirez has put on all October long.
Going back to the final three games of the ALDS, and now Game 1 of the ALCS, Ramirez has simply put Cleveland's lineup on his back.
Terry Francona set it when he managed, and Stephen Vogt has echoed it: when Hosey goes, the Guardians go.
Ramirez is doing more than just swinging a hot bat right now; he's also setting Cleveland franchise history with how much success he's had at the plate so far this postseason.
In the top of the ninth inning on Monday night, Ramirez worked Cole Sulser into a 3-2 count with two outs and Angel Martinez standing on second base. The Tampa Bay pitcher left a cutter up in the zone, and Ramirez took it the other way
Martinez crossed home plate, and the floodgates opened for Cleveland to score two more runs and seal the deal for the Guardians in Game 1.
Looking back to Ramirez, though, this was his eighth hit and eighth RBI of the postseason up to this point.
Ramirez also tied a Cleveland franchise record, becoming just the third player to log an RBI in four straight playoff games. The other two were Jim Thome in 1998-99 and Sandy Alomar in 1997, who still coaches first base for the Guardians.
Ramirez is already one of, if not the best, players in franchise history.
That said, considering the legendary players who played for Cleveland in the 90s, like Albert Belle and Manny Ramirez, along with impressive offensive players in the late 2010s, like Francisco Lindor and Michael Brantley, it really shows how amazing Ramirez is doing.
Whether it's smacking home runs or just getting the ball in play, Vogt said after Game 1 that Ramirez just has a knack for getting on base and making things happen. There's nowhere in the box score or in a stat to measure that impact, but it's real, and the Guardians are feeling it right now.
Vogt went on to talk about how Ramirez's energy "100 percent" feeds off the rest of the team.
Who knows what will happen throughout the rest of the series, but the Guardians should be in a good spot to win the ALCS if Ramirez continues to play at this level.

Guardians vs. Rays: A qué hora y dónde ver a Jonathan Aranda en el Juego 2 de la Serie de Campeonato MLB 2026
Te decimos a qué hora y dónde ver en México el Juego 2 de Guardians vs Rays, con el tijuanense Jonathan Aranda buscando ayudar a Tampa Bay a empatar la Serie de Campeonato.
Los Guardianes de Cleveland y los Rays de Tampa Bay disputarán este martes 13 de octubre el Juego 2 de la Serie de Campeonato de la Liga Americana 2026, nuevamente en el Tropicana Field, de St. Petersburg, Florida.
Cleveland llega con ventaja de 1-0 en la serie, después de remontar y llevarse el primer encuentro por 7-3, por lo que Tampa Bay está obligado a reaccionar antes de que la eliminatoria se traslade a Ohio.
El partido tendrá especial interés para los aficionados mexicanos por la participación del tijuanense Jonathan Aranda, quien intentará recuperar su producción ofensiva después de quedarse sin imparables en el primer encuentro.
Te decimos a qué hora comienza, dónde verlo EN VIVO y quiénes serán los pitchers abridores.
¿Cuándo y a qué hora juegan Guardians vs. Rays el Juego 2 de la Serie de Campeonato 2026?
El segundo encuentro de la Serie de Campeonato de la Liga Americana se disputará este martes 13 de octubre de 2026, con Tampa Bay como local.
Estos son los horarios para las cuatro zonas de México:
- Hora del centro de México: 6:00 PM.
- Hora del noroeste: 5:00 PM.
- Hora del Pacífico: 5:00 PM.
- Hora del sureste: 7:00 PM.
El encuentro se celebrará en el Tropicana Field, donde los Rays intentarán aprovechar su condición de locales para empatar la serie antes de viajar a Cleveland.
¿Dónde ver EN VIVO Guardians vs. Rays, Juego 2, en México?
Los aficionados mexicanos podrán seguir el enfrentamiento de la Serie de Campeonato de la Liga Americana mediante televisión de paga y servicios de streaming.
Las opciones de transmisión para México son:
- TV abierta: No disponible.
- TV de paga: ESPN.
- Streaming: Disney+ y MLB.TV, sujeto a las condiciones de suscripción y disponibilidad regional.
En Estados Unidos, las transmisiones oficiales están programadas por TBS, truTV, HBO Max y UniMás.
¿Cómo quedó el Juego 1 entre Guardians y Rays en la Serie de Campeonato?
Los Guardianes de Cleveland sorprendieron a Tampa Bay en el primer compromiso, disputado el lunes 12 de octubre, al conseguir una remontada que terminó con marcador de 7-3.
Los Rays comenzaron con ventaja de 2-0 en la primera entrada, gracias a sencillos productores de Junior Caminero y Jonny DeLuca. Durante las primeras cinco entradas, el abridor Drew Rasmussen mantuvo controlada a la ofensiva de Cleveland.
Sin embargo, los Guardianes comenzaron su reacción en la sexta entrada con un cuadrangular solitario de Chase DeLauter, mientras que Patrick Bailey conectó otro jonrón en el séptimo episodio para empatar el marcador.
El batazo decisivo llegó en la octava entrada, cuando Nathaniel Lowe conectó un sencillo productor de dos carreras que puso a Cleveland adelante por 4-2.
Aunque Cedric Mullins acercó a los Rays con un cuadrangular solitario, Cleveland agregó tres anotaciones en la novena entrada para asegurar el triunfo.
Con esta victoria, los Guardianes llegaron a cuatro triunfos consecutivos en la postemporada, contando los últimos tres encuentros que ganaron frente a los Medias Blancas de Chicago.
¿Cómo llega Jonathan Aranda al Juego 2 con los Rays de Tampa Bay?
El mexicano Jonathan Aranda, originario de Tijuana, Baja California, buscará recuperar el protagonismo que tuvo durante la Serie Divisional contra los Yankees de Nueva York.
En el primer partido frente a Cleveland, Aranda apareció como segundo bate y primera base de los Rays, pero terminó sin hits en tres turnos oficiales, con un ponche.
No obstante, el mexicano contribuyó a la primera carrera de Tampa Bay mediante un toque de sacrificio que permitió a Yandy Díaz avanzar hasta la tercera base en el primer episodio.
Aranda llegó a la Serie de Campeonato después de registrar una destacada actuación contra los Yankees, a quienes los Rays eliminaron por barrida de 3-0.
Durante aquella eliminatoria, el tijuanense conectó cuatro imparables en 12 turnos, con promedio de .333, un cuadrangular y dos carreras impulsadas.
Su batazo más importante fue un jonrón solitario contra Gerrit Cole, que representó la única anotación en la victoria de Tampa Bay por 1-0 en el primer encuentro de la Serie Divisional.
Además, Aranda terminó la temporada regular de MLB 2026 con 22 cuadrangulares y 92 carreras impulsadas, consolidándose como una de las piezas más importantes de la ofensiva dirigida por Kevin Cash.
Para el Juego 2, el mexicano tendrá enfrente a un lanzador zurdo, por lo que su participación será importante en los ajustes ofensivos que busquen los Rays.
¿Quiénes serán los pitchers abridores del Juego 2 entre Guardians y Rays?
Los equipos tienen definidos a los lanzadores encargados de iniciar el segundo encuentro de la Serie de Campeonato.
Parker Messick (Guardians de Cleveland)
El lanzador zurdo será el encargado de abrir por Cleveland, con la misión de contener a una ofensiva que cuenta con bateadores como Jonathan Aranda, Junior Caminero y Yandy Díaz.
Messick tiene marca de 0-1, efectividad de 5.40 y 11 ponches durante la postemporada de 2026.
Su actuación será importante para unos Guardianes que buscan regresar a casa con ventaja de dos victorias en la eliminatoria.
Freddy Peralta (Rays de Tampa Bay)
Tampa Bay enviará a la lomita al derecho Freddy Peralta, quien intentará igualar la Serie de Campeonato.
Peralta llega con récord de 0-0, efectividad de 1.93 y tres ponches en esta postemporada.
El abridor tendrá la responsabilidad de frenar a una ofensiva de Cleveland que conectó 14 imparables durante el primer encuentro, encabezada por José Ramírez, Chase DeLauter y Nathaniel Lowe.
¿Qué necesitan los Rays para empatar la Serie de Campeonato contra Cleveland?
Tampa Bay necesita ganar el encuentro de este martes para colocar la Serie de Campeonato 1-1, antes de disputar los siguientes partidos como visitante.
Los Rays finalizaron la temporada regular con 98 victorias y 64 derrotas, el mejor récord de la Liga Americana, además de eliminar por barrida a los Yankees en la Serie Divisional.
Sin embargo, en el primer enfrentamiento contra Cleveland dejaron escapar una ventaja de dos carreras y su cuerpo de relevistas no logró contener a los bateadores rivales durante las últimas entradas.
Por su parte, los Guardianes llegan con la motivación de haber remontado una desventaja de 0-2 contra los White Sox para ganar tres encuentros consecutivos y avanzar a esta instancia.
Si Cleveland consigue otra victoria, regresará al Progressive Field con ventaja de 2-0 y la posibilidad de conquistar el campeonato de la Liga Americana ante sus propios aficionados.
En cambio, una victoria de Tampa Bay garantizaría que la serie viaje a Ohio empatada, dejando abierta la lucha por el boleto a la Serie Mundial 2026.
¿Cuál es el calendario completo de Guardians vs. Rays en la Serie de Campeonato 2026?
La Serie de Campeonato de la Liga Americana se disputa al mejor de siete encuentros, por lo que el primer equipo que consiga cuatro victorias avanzará a la Serie Mundial.

Los Juegos 5, 6 y 7 solamente se disputarán en caso de ser necesarios. La MLB también contempla posibles modificaciones de horario dependiendo del desarrollo de las Series de Campeonato.
El ganador de esta eliminatoria enfrentará al campeón de la Liga Nacional, que saldrá de la serie entre Dodgers de Los Ángeles y Cerveceros de Milwaukee, por el título de la Serie Mundial 2026.

item.content:encoded:
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. – The Cleveland Guardians used small ball, the longball and played solid all-around baseball to keep winning in the postseason.
Nathaniel Lowe snapped an eighth-inning tie with a two-run single after Chase DeLauter and Patrick Bailey homered off Drew Rasmussen, and the Guardians rallied past the Tampa Bay Rays 7-3 in Game 1 of the American League Championship Series on Monday night.
Recommended Videos
After losing the first two games at home to the Chicago White Sox in their AL Division Series, Cleveland has won four straight in the postseason for the first time since winning their first six playoff games in 2016 on the way to a World Series berth.
“It feels good to see some balls fall, to see some guys get on the barrel, to see some guys have some great at-bats, because the first two games of the White Sox series, we got beat. We did,” Lowe said. “We had to go get our backs against the wall and do something crazy, and this group did. It’s nice to feel some momentum coming here and to take Game 1.”
Jose Ramírez had three hits and DeLauter was a triple shy of the cycle as the Guardians banged out 14 hits against a Tampa Bay staff that allowed just 12 in its entire Division Series against the New York Yankees.
Junior Caminero and Jonny DeLuca had RBI singles in the first and Cedric Mullins hit a solo homer for the Rays, who never trailed in their three-game sweep of the Yankees.
“It’s been a while since we lost, so I think that’s a good thing, and I know the guys will come back and respond tomorrow,” Tampa Bay manager Kevin Cash said.
Game 2 is Tuesday night at Tropicana Field. Rookie left-hander Parker Messick starts for Cleveland, and right-hander Freddy Peralta takes the mound for the Rays.
Five relievers combined for five innings of one-run, two-hit ball for the Guardians, who became only the 11th team to overcome an 0-2 deficit in a best-of-five playoff series with a victory over the White Sox on Saturday night.
Hunter Gaddis worked a scoreless seventh for the win. Cade Smith, who pitched in all five games against Chicago, tossed a perfect ninth.
“Obviously we came off an emotional series, had a quick turnaround. But these guys come ready to play every day. Couldn’t be more proud of them,” Cleveland manager Stephen Vogt said. “We got punched early. And our pitching staff, credit to them, for stopping it and keeping us in the game as long as they did. And the offense came alive.”
Rasmussen took a 2-0 lead into the sixth before DeLauter led off with an opposite-field homer to left-center. Bailey started the seventh with a towering shot to center that went a projected 436 feet, ending Rasmussen’s night.
Rasmussen carried a no-hitter into the eighth in Game 1 of the ALDS against the Yankees.
Ramírez opened the eighth with an infield single off losing pitcher Tyler Wells, and DeLauter ripped a double to right. After Wells retired Jo Adell on a grounder to second, Ian Seymour entered. Lowe lined an 0-2 pitch up the middle to drive in two, giving Cleveland a 4-2 lead.
Lowe made his major league debut with Tampa Bay in 2019 and won a World Series with Texas in 2023.
“I love coming back here, I really do,” Lowe said. “It’s nice to see some familiar faces on the other side.”
Mullins connected off Erik Sabrowski for a solo shot in the bottom half.
Ramírez, whose two-run homer lifted Cleveland to a 2-0 win in Game 5 against Chicago, provided an insurance run with an RBI single in the ninth off Cole Sulser.
Ramírez then helped the Guardians get two more by breaking for third with two outs and two strikes on Adell. Caminero ran to cover the bag and was out of position when Adell hit a sharp grounder toward third. The ball rolled into left field for a two-run double.
A crowd of 35,361 fans waved yellow rally towels and rang cowbells at the Trop as Tampa Bay made its third ALCS appearance in the franchise's 29-season history.
They were fired up when the 98-win Rays jumped ahead 2-0 in the first and Rasmussen battled to keep it there until the sixth.
Coming off that dominant performance against the Yankees, Rasmussen went six-plus tough innings. The two-time All-Star right-hander, who was four outs from a no-hitter in a 1-0 victory against New York, allowed a hit to the second batter he faced and eight total, striking out seven.
Guardians starter Foster Griffin gave up two runs and five hits in four innings.
Glove work
The Rays helped Rasmussen with outstanding defense.
Nick Fortes threw out Ramírez trying to steal second in the first. Caminero made an excellent play to retire Adell on a hard bouncer to third. Caminero short-hopped the ball with his backhand and fired a strong throw to first.
The Guardians had a runner on first with one out in the third when second baseman Ben Williamson robbed DeLauter of a hit that prevented a first-and-third jam. Williamson, who wasn’t on the ALDS roster, made a diving grab on DeLauter’s sharp grounder, got up and threw him out.
Stranded runners
Rays slick-fielding shortstop Taylor Walls was 0 for 3 and left six runners on base. He struck out with the bases loaded to end the first, lined out with a runner on in the fourth and grounded out with runners on first and second to end the sixth.
Up next
Messick took the loss in Game 1 of the AL Division Series, allowing two runs over 4 1/3 innings. He threw 2 1/3 innings in relief during a Game 4 victory, giving up two runs. Messick had 11 strikeouts in the two appearances. He was 12-9 with a 2.56 ERA in the regular season.
Peralta allowed one run and three hits over 4 2/3 innings in Game 2 of the Division Series vs. the Yankees. He was 5-2 with a 3.25 ERA in 10 starts after joining Tampa Bay at the trade deadline. Peralta was 5-9 with a 4.99 ERA for the Mets this season.

If Boston Red Sox fans are still watching the Major League Baseball postseason, they're probably picking up on some reasons their team didn't make it this far.
Though the Red Sox had one magical stretch of 32-5 baseball this season, it was painfully obvious by the time they finished their Wild Card Series at Yankee Stadium that they were never built for a deep playoff run. And the way their offense functioned in that series was a microcosm of the season.
When the chips were on the table, the Red Sox couldn't put anyone next to Willson Contreras in the lineup that was capable of inflicting damage. Even with a bum hand, Contreras hit well enough in that series to help the team move on — it was just that all of his teammates failed to rise to the task.
Red Sox fall short of other lineup cores
The teams still playing all have some sort of dynamic duo, trio, or better in their lineup. The Milwaukee Brewers have Jackson Chourio, Brice Turang, and William Contreras. The Los Angeles Dodgers have the most star-studded lineup we've ever seen, with $60 million man Kyle Tucker batting eighth.
The Tampa Bay Rays have Yandy Díaz and Jonathan Aranda providing thump in front of Junior Caminero. Even the Cleveland Guardians have a strong supporting cast around José Ramírez, with Steven Kwan getting on base, Jo Adell driving balls in the gap, and Chase DeLauter lurking.
But in the Wild Card Series, as soon as it was clear that Roman Anthony's hand was toast, the Red Sox had no other threats in front of or behind Contreras. Adley Rutschman's at-bats got worse as the series went along, while Wilyer Abreu and Ceddanne Rafaela looked absolutely lost in the batter's box.
There's a lesson to be learned here. Even if the Red Sox feel good about the steps forward some of their hitters can take from this season into next, it seems imperative at this point to add another star-caliber bat. And that's not going to be easy, given the impending lockout and soft free agency class.
Whether it's buying high on Randy Arozarena or further depleting the farm system for Hunter Goodman, the Red Sox are going to have to do something uncomfortable to give themselves a real shot at contention.

My expectation going into this exercise was that third base would be terrible, clearly the worst position for Fantasy in 2027. Now, I'm not sure.
It's bad, yes, offering only six players that I'd feel great about drafting, but having just ranked second base a few days ago ... I don't know. Third base might be better.
- Early rankings: | | | 3B | SS | OF | SP | RP
Just look at the crossover players. Bryson Stott ranked 11th for me at second base. He's 16th here. Javier Sanoja, Willi Castro and Ezequiel Duran all placed in my top 20 at second base. None of them do here.
Second base may have safer options, by and large, but there's more upside to be found at third base. And while second base is losing a whole host of players due to eligibility restrictions, only one of real significance, Jazz Chisholm, is dropping out at third.
Note that the focus here is standard 5x5 scoring (such as Rotisserie leagues), but scroll a little further, and you'll see my rankings for points leagues as well.
| 1 | |
| Whatever doubts existed for Caminero heading into 2026 were thoroughly expunged by a second consecutive 40-homer campaign in which he nearly doubled his walk rate -- a telltale sign that he's now among the most feared hitters in the game. At 23, he's poised for a lengthy reign atop this position. | |
| 2 | |
| Between the massive increase in average bat speed and the pull-air rate verging on 30 percent, there's little reason to doubt Vargas' power contributions, and he's fast enough to continue impacting the stolen base category as well. Some will be inclined toward skepticism given the enormity of his breakthrough, but third base unfortunately doesn't allow for such nitpicking. | |
| 3 | |
| Stewart's totals were more impressive than his percentages in 2026, which could make him a polarizing player heading into the new season, but based on his minor league numbers, I think he has more ground to gain in strikeouts and pull-air rate. The 15 steals are the most iffy part of his 2026 stat line, judging by his 27th percentile sprint speed. | |
| 4 | |
| Ramirez's power completely vanished in the second half, when he hit just two home runs, which is concerning enough to dethrone him at the position he has long dominated. He does have a valid excuse for it, seeing as he was coming off a broken hamate bone during that time, and I'll note that his contact skills and base-stealing remained perfectly intact. Still, he doesn't get the full benefit of the doubt at age 34. | |
| 5 | |
| After a sluggish opening act in Chicago that positioned him to be a free agent bust, Bregman made some mechanical changes midseason that led to the sort of power production we hadn't seen from him since his 41-homer 2019. While the .317 batting average, 17 homers and 1.103 OPS that he delivered over his final 43 games isn't projectable over a full season, it makes him out to be a trustworthy choice at this thin position. | |
| 6 | |
| McGonigle had a historic rookie season in many ways, but not necessarily the most Fantasy-friendly ways, owing much to his superlative defense and on-base skills. How much power he can pack onto his 5-foot-9 frame, particularly at a restrictive venue, will go a long way toward determining his ceiling. Still, he has ground to gain in batting average and stolen bases. | |
| 7 | |
| The decline for Machado in 2026, while marked, was mostly restricted to batting average, which normally isn't the first indicator of a player aging out. But he is 34 and had only one month (July) with an OPS of .800 or better. I suspect that his issues were mostly mechanical, but it's hard to take a glass-half-full approach with him when he still commands a premium at the position. | |
| 8 | |
| Gelof faked us out once before with a splashy rookie showing in 2023, but his success in 2026 went beyond just the surface level. He added more than 2 mph in average bat speed and shaved more than 10 points off his strikeout rate from the previous two years. Of course, he missed some time with injuries, but if you project his 22 homers and 16 steals over 162 games, they come out to 32 homers and 23 steals. | |
