| If Okamoto simply repeats his 2026 stat line, he'll be well worth drafting here, but that's a big if. The league learned to force-feed him breaking balls, diminishing his power over the course of the year, and his poor batting average and uninspired defense already give him a thin margin for error. His success depends on him piling up counting stats, so any threat to his playing time could be a deal-breaker. | |
| 10 | |
| An early injury to Carlos Correa conferred everyday duty upon Paredes, and it went about as swimmingly as it always does for him, which hopefully means the playing time question won't be raised again. He has little raw power but excels at lofting the ball to the shallowest part of left field, which is generally good for 25-plus home runs, particularly with the Crawford Boxes at his disposal in Houston. His plate discipline elevates him all the more in points leagues. | |
| 11 | |
| Muncy played in a career-high 149 games in 2026 and performed equally against righties and lefties, which may be enough to quiet the talk of decline. Seeing as he's 36, though, it's still going to be on the tip of everyone's tongue, and just because he performed adequately versus lefties doesn't mean the Dodgers were eager to use him against them. The profile is similar to Isaac Paredes, but I think with more playing time risk. | |
| 12 | |
| Improved pull-air and strikeout rates put Mead on the breakout path with a .253/.353/.498 slash line. It also compelled the Red Sox to give up an intriguing young hurler ( Connelly Early ) for him at the trade deadline. They have yet to see any benefit since he got hurt right away. However, Mead is in line to start for them at second base, which would only expand his already favorable eligibility. His swing should theoretically play well at Fenway Park, but he remains largely unproven. | |
| 13 | |
| Like Curtis Mead Schmitt's breakout was interrupted by a midseason injury (torn meniscus), and in some ways, it was the more compelling of the two. He picked up 1 mph in average bat speed and had an xBA (.288) and xSLG (.512) that were 95th percentile or better. He has a tendency to swing at everything, though, which leaves him vulnerable to the right game plan. Also, while Mead's home venue is likely to help, Schmitt's is likely to hurt. | |
| 14 | |
| It's hard to keep giving Bichette the benefit of the doubt when he fails us twice in three years, and by ranking him this low at a weak position, I would say that I'm not. But I'm also not burying him for three reasons: He hit .284 with a .772 OPS over the final four months, was reportedly still feeling the effects of a PCL sprain early in the year, and will only be 29 next year. It's a batting average-dependent profile, and those can be volatile. | |
| 15 | |
| It's even harder to give Riley the benefit of the doubt now that his numbers have declined five straight years, with the biggest drop coming in 2026, but by golly, he still hits the ball hard. The jump in chase rate this year suggests that his issues are more related to mechanics or approach than diminished tools, which leaves the door open for a fix. It's a long shot, of course, but it's glimmer enough for a budget corner infield pick, particularly with his kind of upside. | |
| 16 | |
| Stott ranks 11th for me at second base, which makes a compelling case that it's actually the weaker position, despite third base's reputation. His upside is more limited than the four ahead of him here. Still, I could see him leapfrogging them on Draft Day, depending on how the scarcities shake out (not just positionally but also statistically, with him being a superior base-stealer). | |
| 17 | |
| The jump from seven home runs to 16 made Garcia a premier third baseman in 2025, so when he regressed to only three (albeit in 82 games) the following year, it's probably reason enough to dismiss him as a one-hit wonder. Trouble is that all three came before he suffered a hand injury in mid-May, and I'm not sure he was ever quite right thereafter, needing separate IL stints for the injury. That he stopped stealing bases is another concern, though. | |
| 18 | |
| Arenado seemed to be on his way out as a power hitter, his dwindling exit velocities reaching a tipping point as he failed to deliver 20 homers in consecutive seasons, and this made it all the more shocking to see him bounce back with 30 this year, 16 of which came in the final two months. I'm skeptical of a repeat, both because he's in his mid-30s and because his average exit velocity actually diminished further to the 3rd percentile. If the Diamondbacks are at all to credit for the turnaround, he'll surely enjoy having another season with them. | |
| 19 | |
| Availability can sometimes trump ability, and simply by virtue of starting 151 games for the Twins (and coming off the bench in five others), Lee compiled some pretty good totals in 2026. The only area where you might consider him a plus, though, is home runs, and those came more from an optimal pull-air rate than a natural ability to impact a baseball. Any slippage in health or production would reduce him to mediocrity again.  | |
| 20 | |
| Westburg spent all of 2026 recovering from a UCL tear, submitting to full-blown Tommy John surgery in May, but since he's a hitter and not a pitcher, he should be in pretty good shape come spring training. The 27-year-old was a burgeoning power threat prior to the procedure, showing the capacity for 30-plus homers in a healthy season, and isn't near the batting average liability that, say, Colson Montgomery is. | |

Estados Unidos/Los Guardianes de Cleveland iniciarán el lunes frente a los Rays de Tampa Bay la Serie de Campeonato de la Liga Americana con la esperanza de poner fin a una sequía de títulos que se remonta a 1948, la más prolongada actualmente en las Grandes Ligas.
Cleveland eliminó el sábado a los Medias Blancas de Chicago tras remontar para ganar los tres últimos partidos de la serie divisional y avanzar a una nueva instancia decisiva.
Los Guardianes, que adoptaron su actual nombre tras abandonar el de Indians al término de la temporada 2021, no disputan una Serie Mundial desde 2016.
Te puede interesar: MLB Playoffs 2026 resultado| Guardianes se impulsan con jonrón de Ramirez hacia la Serie de Campeonato de la Liga Americana
"La mentalidad es siempre la misma, sin importar el resultado. Así es el béisbol", dijo el antesalista dominicano José Ramírez. "Siempre hay que encontrar la manera de ganar, y eso es lo que ha hecho este grupo: encontrar las formas de ganar".
"Y para nosotros seguirá siendo lo mismo: encontrar formas de ganar y cómo podemos pasar a la siguiente ronda", sostuvo el quisqueyano.
La última aparición de Cleveland en una Serie Mundial terminó con una dolorosa derrota ante los Cachorros de Chicago en siete partidos, una definición que puso fin a una histórica sequía de 108 años para la franquicia rival.
Los Guardianes también cayeron en la Serie Mundial de 1997 frente a los entonces Marlins de Florida.

- El sueño pendiente de los Rays -
Del otro lado estará un equipo que persigue el primer campeonato de su historia. Fundados en 1998, los Rays jamás han conquistado una Serie Mundial.
Tampa Bay llega además como el mejor equipo de la Liga Americana en la temporada regular, con una marca de 98 victorias y 64 derrotas, frente al registro de 85-77 de Cleveland.
Los Rays dominaron claramente los cruces entre ambos conjuntos durante la fase regular al ganar cinco de los seis enfrentamientos y superar a los Guardianes por 20 carreras contra ocho.
Sin embargo, tres de esos encuentros se decidieron por una sola carrera.
"En lo que respecta a los Guardianes, se siente como una serie contra los Yankees, en la que los partidos siempre son reñidos", dijo el mánager de Tampa Bay, Kevin Cash.

"Muy bien jugados. Muy bien lanzados. Grandes hits en el momento oportuno", agregó el piloto.
El jardinero Ryan Vilade destacó la unión del plantel como una de las claves de la campaña de los Rays.
"Este equipo, este grupo, estamos muy unidos. Nos animamos unos a otros con mucha fuerza", dijo Vilade.
"Jugamos unos por otros y creo que eso es lo que lo hace especial. Somos un grupo de luchadores. Vamos a salir al campo. No nos importa quién esté del otro lado. Vamos a salir a competir, a hacer lo nuestro, a ser nosotros mismos y a no intentar hacer más de lo necesario".
El campeón de la Liga Americana enfrentará en la Serie Mundial al vencedor de la Liga Nacional, donde los Cerveceros de Milwaukee y los Dodgers de Los Ángeles siguen en carrera por el título.

CLEVELAND -- This must be how it had to be.
The White Sox and Guardians have exhausted each other all year. They played 13 times in the regular season, with seven games decided by one run and four ending with a walk-off. Their AL Central battle came down to a single game. And now, their best-of-five ALDS has reached a decisive Game 5 on Saturday night, at what will be a packed and passionate Progressive Field.
These teams’ scouting reports on each other are so detailed at this point that they include players’ childhood fears and preferred orders at the airport Cinnabon. There are old married couples that haven’t spent as much time together as the 2026 Sox and Guardians.
But only one of them can advance to face the No. 1-seeded Rays in the ALCS, which begins Monday at Tropicana Field. And with both Chicago and Cleveland having won two games apiece in the other’s domain, this deeply personal hard-fought series -- the only LDS to go the distance this year -- will now get the winner-take-all it deserves.
“Just on to the next,” White Sox shortstop Colson Montgomery said. “Flush these last two games. It’s out of our control now. All we can control is how we show up on Saturday.”
After Gavin Williams closed out the Guardians’ win in Game 4 with an emergency relief appearance, he will take the ball in Game 5 for his second start this series. Williams, who struck out an AL-best 248 batters in the regular season, struck out 11 more in only five innings in Game 2.
“It's a Game 5, win or go home,” manager Stephen Vogt said. “Gavin wants the ball. We want him to have the ball, and it's his game.”
Give Cleveland credit for pulling itself off the mat in a tough environment on the South Side. José Ramírez roared to life, and a Guards offense that had been flat in Games 1 and 2 scored 18 runs total across Games 3 and 4.
The last team to rally from an 0-2 hole in a best-of-five series and win it was the 2017 Yankees … against Cleveland. The Guardians could join the 2001 Yankees (vs. A’s), 2012 Giants (vs. Reds) and 2015 Blue Jays (vs. Rangers) as the only teams to come back from 0-2 in the Division Series after losing the first two at home. One figures that if the Guardians are going to end the longest active championship drought in the sport (dating back to 1948), they might as well do it the hard way.
“I think momentum's definitely going be big in this next one,” Steven Kwan said. “We kind of let the home crowd down those first two games. So hopefully it's another chance at redemption.”
As for the Sox, they missed their chance to clinch a playoff series at home for the first time since 1906. But that trivia is trivial compared to the ultimate goal of reaching the next round in any way, shape or form. No one expected Chicago to even reach the playoffs this year, but this No. 6-seeded team has made serious noise with its unorthodox pitching plan. And as bad as things went at home, at least they come into Game 5 with their best starter, Sean Burke, rested and ready.
“Play our baseball,” White Sox second baseman Chase Meidroth said. “Some at-bats we bounced back and had some good little runs. Couldn’t get that big hit. But they are a good staff and a great pitching staff. It’s not easy, it’s not easy against them ever.”
This exhausting, exhilarating AL Central rivalry has one game left to play. It’s the Central focus of the baseball world.
When is the game and how can I tune in?
Game 5 of the ALDS presented by Booking.com is scheduled for Saturday at 8 ET/7 CT on TBS/truTV/UniMas/HBO Max.
The ALDS will be available in Spanish on UniMas, while Univision’s TUDN Radio will provide Spanish-language audio coverage. ESPN Radio will provide live national coverage of all 2026 MLB Postseason games.
Who are the starting pitchers?
White Sox manager Will Venable committed to Burke starting Game 5 during a Friday afternoon Zoom session from Rate Field. The right-hander had a 2-0 record with a 1.04 ERA in three regular-season appearances (two starts) against the Guardians, so the White Sox have to feel confident.
Key stat: Williams is coming off his first relief appearance at any level as a professional. Before that, his previous bullpen experience came in 2021 while in college at East Carolina.
The Guardians’ advantage in earning a postseason first-round bye was their ability to get Parker Messick and Williams two starts apiece in the ALDS. Ironically, Messick’s 2 1/3-inning effort in Game 4 prompted an unplanned bullpen game in which Cleveland used seven additional pitchers -- including Williams, who got the final three outs.
Vogt on Friday announced Williams, who threw 18 pitches, will be his Game 5 starter.
“After the game last night, I was walking by his office and I told him I was ready to go,” Williams said Friday. “Whatever [I need to do] to help the team win, that's what I'm going to do. It doesn't matter the role at this point.”
What do the starting lineups look like?
White Sox: With the right-handed throwing power of Williams potentially on the mound, look for Venable to go back to his left-handed directed lineup.
Guardians: Patrick Bailey figures to be back behind the plate after he went 2-for-3 with a pinch-hit home run and two RBIs in Game 4. It will be curious if the Guardians make a switch in the outfield, given Angel Martínez is 0-for-15 with eight strikeouts this series. Daniel Schneemann, Petey Halpin and David Fry each are options on the ALDS roster.
How will the bullpens line up after the starter?
White Sox: Grant Taylor explained after Thursday’s rough showing (where he faced six hitters and didn’t retire any of them) how he will be ready to throw Saturday in any form even if it’s nine innings. The White Sox will be using whomever they have available, whether it’s relievers or starters, to get through Game 5.
Guardians: Whoever advances to the ALCS will do so with a pitching staff that has carried a heavy workload this series. The Guardians will worry about Game 1 of that series if they are fortunate to get there, Vogt said Thursday night. It will be all hands on deck coming out of the off-day on Friday.
“Obviously we need to see how everybody feels today,” Vogt said Friday. “We need to see how everybody feels coming in tomorrow. But I think if you're a pitcher on our roster, be ready to go tomorrow.”
Any injuries of note?
White Sox: None.
Guardians: Austin Hedges took a Teel foul tip off his right knee in the second inning in Game 4. He was sore on Friday, Vogt said, but the skipper expressed optimism Hedges will be ready to go on Saturday.
Who is hot and who is not?
White Sox: Miguel Vargas homered in the ninth inning off Cade Smith Thursday and reached base three other times via the walk. Munetaka Murakami singled while also walking twice.
Anything else fans might want to know?
- Vargas has reached base 12 times in total during the series.
- Bailey’s pinch-hit homer in the fifth inning of Game 4 was the first by the Guardians in the postseason since Jhonkensy Noel in Game 3 of the 2024 ALCS.

¿Quién es José Ramírez? El dominicano que salvó a los Guardianes y forzó el Juego 5 ante los Medias Blancas
El tercera base dominicano José Ramírez conectó un jonrón de dos carreras y remolcó tres anotaciones en la victoria 9-5 de Cleveland sobre Chicago. El triunfo mantiene con vida a los Guardianes y lleva la Serie Divisional de la Liga Americana a un quinto y decisivo encuentro.
Foto: ¿Quién es José Ramírez? El dominicano que salvó a los Guardianes y forzó el Juego 5 ante los Medias Blancas.
Cuando Cleveland más necesitaba una respuesta, Ramírez volvió a hacerse sentir. El dominicano conectó un cuadrangular clave en el quinto episodio y contribuyó a la remontada que permitió al conjunto igualar la serie a dos victorias por bando, el jueves 8 de octubre.

El resultado cambió el panorama de una eliminatoria que se había complicado para los Guardianes tras perder los dos primeros partidos en casa. Ahora, el equipo tendrá la oportunidad de definir su clasificación ante su público, con un boleto a la Serie de Campeonato de la Liga Americana en juego.
José Ramírez, una estrella dominicana en Cleveland
José Enrique Ramírez nació el 17 de septiembre de 1992 en Baní, República Dominicana. Conocido también como «Enriquito», se ha consolidado como una de las figuras más importantes de los Guardianes de Cleveland, equipo con el que debutó en las Grandes Ligas el 1 de septiembre de 2013.
Aunque su posición habitual es la tercera base, su aporte ofensivo lo ha convertido en mucho más que un defensor del cuadro interior. A lo largo de su carrera, ha destacado por su capacidad para producir carreras, conectar extrabases y aprovechar su velocidad en las bases.
El dominicano ha sido seleccionado siete veces al Juego de Estrellas y ha obtenido varios reconocimientos individuales, entre ellos el Bate de Plata. En 2025 también ocupó el tercer lugar en la votación para el Jugador Más Valioso de la Liga Americana, un reconocimiento que refleja su relevancia en la competición.
Su trayectoria en Cleveland abarca más de una década, período en el que pasó de ser un joven con proyección a convertirse en uno de los principales referentes ofensivos de la franquicia.
Te puede interesar: ¿Qué partidos de MLB se juegan este fin de semana? Horarios y dónde verlos en RD los días 9 al 11 de octubre de 2026
El jonrón que cambió el rumbo del partido
El cuarto encuentro ante Chicago exigía una reacción inmediata de los Guardianes. Después de comenzar la serie con dos derrotas, Cleveland había ganado el tercer partido por 9-3 y necesitaba otra victoria para evitar la eliminación.
La ofensiva volvió a encontrar su ritmo, aunque el desenlace estuvo lejos de quedar definido desde el principio. En el quinto episodio, Cleveland comenzó a construir su remontada y Ramírez protagonizó uno de los batazos más importantes de la noche.
El dominicano se enfrentó al lanzador derecho Jordan Hicks y, con un compañero en circulación, conectó una recta de 99.9 millas por hora. La pelota salió hacia el jardín derecho-central y terminó fuera del parque, dándole a Cleveland una ventaja de 3-2.
El batazo tuvo un significado especial por la velocidad del lanzamiento que logró convertir en cuadrangular. Además, representó su primer jonrón de postemporada desde 2024.
Chicago respondió en la parte baja de esa misma entrada y recuperó la ventaja, lo que volvió a poner a los Guardianes bajo presión. Sin embargo, la ofensiva de Cleveland todavía tenía mucho por aportar y encontró otra oportunidad para cambiar el curso del encuentro.
Seis carreras en una entrada para seguir con vida
El momento decisivo llegó en el sexto episodio, cuando los Guardianes enviaron a diez bateadores al plato y fabricaron seis carreras para tomar una ventaja que ya no perderían.
La reacción comenzó con Ángel Martínez, quien recibió un pelotazo y se robó una base antes de anotar gracias a un doble impulsor de Travis Bazzana. A partir de ahí, Cleveland aprovechó nuevas oportunidades con imparables y boletos que aumentaron la presión sobre el cuerpo de lanzadores de Chicago.
Ramírez también volvió a responder con un sencillo productor, completando una actuación de dos imparables en cinco turnos, un cuadrangular y tres carreras impulsadas.
Ese episodio terminó siendo determinante para sellar el triunfo por 9-5. Los Guardianes no solo evitaron la eliminación, sino que consiguieron su segunda victoria consecutiva como visitantes, después de comenzar la serie con dos derrotas en su estadio.
Aunque el protagonismo se repartió entre varios integrantes de la alineación, la producción del antesalista dominicano contribuyó a cambiar la dinámica del partido. Su capacidad para conectar batazos oportunos llegó en un momento en el que el equipo necesitaba aprovechar cada oportunidad para mantenerse en la lucha.
Un líder en los momentos de presión
La actuación de Ramírez vuelve a poner de relieve su importancia dentro de la franquicia. Durante años, el dominicano ha sido una pieza fundamental en las aspiraciones de Cleveland y continúa protagonizando actuaciones relevantes en la postemporada.
Su experiencia cobra especial valor en una serie que ha exigido ajustes constantes y capacidad de reacción después de cada derrota. Tras quedar abajo 0-2, los Guardianes ganaron los dos encuentros siguientes y recuperaron sus posibilidades de avanzar a la siguiente ronda.
No obstante, la remontada todavía está incompleta. El quinto partido determinará cuál de los dos equipos continuará su camino hacia el título de la Liga Americana, por lo que Cleveland necesitará mantener el ritmo ofensivo y reducir los errores para aprovechar la ventaja de jugar en casa.
Te puede interesar: Playoffs MLB 2026: los equipos favoritos para llegar a la Serie Mundial
¿Cuándo se juega el Juego 5 entre Guardianes y Medias Blancas?
El quinto encuentro está programado para el sábado 10 de octubre, a las 8:00 de la noche, hora del Este de Estados Unidos, en el Progressive Field de Cleveland.
El ganador avanzará a la Serie de Campeonato de la Liga Americana, donde se enfrentará a los Rays de Tampa Bay, que esperan al vencedor de esta eliminatoria.
Para Ramírez y sus compañeros, el triunfo del jueves representa una nueva oportunidad después de quedar al borde de la eliminación. El dominicano ya hizo su aporte con un cuadrangular decisivo y tres carreras impulsadas, pero ahora los Guardianes tendrán que completar la remontada en un partido que definirá su continuidad en la postemporada.

CHICAGO -- Jose Ramirez homered and drove in three runs, and the Cleveland Guardians beat the Chicago White Sox 9-5 on Thursday night to send their American League division series to a winner-takes-all Game 5.
Pinch-hitter Patrick Bailey also went deep as the Guardians won for the second consecutive day after beginning their postseason with two straight losses at home. Jo Adell hit a two-run single to cap a six-run sixth inning for the AL Central champions.
Cleveland is looking to become the first major league team to come back from a 2-0 deficit in a best-of-five playoff series since the 2017 New York Yankees accomplished the feat against, well, Cleveland. Teams with a 2-0 lead in a best-of-five postseason series have gone on to win 83 of 93 times.
Game 5 is back in Cleveland on Saturday night.
Chicago's bullpen -- one of its biggest strengths in a surprising season -- is suddenly looking very tired. Grant Taylor was hit hard after pitching 5 1/3 scoreless innings over the first two games of the series, allowing four runs and four hits without retiring any of the six batters he faced during Cleveland's rally in the sixth.
Miguel Vargas homered late for the White Sox, who flopped in their second straight bid to clinch a postseason series at home for the first time since the 1906 World Series against the Chicago Cubs. Sam Antonacci drove in two runs.
Game 2 starter Gavin Williams got the last three outs for Cleveland after Vargas began the ninth with his first postseason homer. It was the first career relief appearance for Williams, who could start Game 5 for the Guardians.
Cleveland trailed 2-0 before rallying in the fifth. Bailey led off with a pinch-hit homer, and Steven Kwan chased Erick Fedde with a one-out single.
Jordan Hicks came in and Ramirez drove a 99.9 mph fastball deep to right-center for just his second homer since Sept. 1, a span of 26 games. The seven-time All-Star had surgery after he broke a bone in his left hand on a swing June 13.
It was Ramirez's first postseason homer since 2024 and No. 5 overall. He also starred in Game 3, finishing with two hits and two RBis in Cleveland's 9-3 victory.
Chicago responded with two runs in the bottom half, sending a charge through the crowd of 39,920. Anthony Kay started the sixth for Chicago, but the left-hander was replaced by Taylor after Travis Bazzana's RBI double tied it at 4-4. Bailey greeted Taylor with a run-scoring single, and Cleveland started to pull away.
Walks by Brayan Rocchio and Kwan loaded the bases for Ramirez, who made it 6-4 with an infield single. Chase DeLauter added another run-scoring single before Adell capped the outburst with a liner to right that drove in Kwan and Ramirez.

CHICAGO — Even in the worst full season of his career, a true superstar can turn it on at any time.
José Ramírez is arguably one of the five best players in Major League Baseball. He had a down year by his standards in 2026, but the Cleveland Guardians couldn't have picked a better time for their best player to get hot. With their season on the line in Game 4 of the ALDS against the Chicago White Sox and an opportunity to send the series back to Cleveland for a winner-take-all Game 5, the Guardians' superman found his cape.
"That's a future Hall of Famer," outfielder Chase DeLauter said after Cleveland's 9-5 victory on Thursday in Chicago. "It's special."
Through the first two games of the ALDS, Ramírez didn't look like the player Cleveland knows him to be, going 0-for-6 with three strikeouts. His early-series struggles seemingly carried over from the final month of the regular season, which saw him put up a paltry .198/.237/.264 slashline with just one home run.
But Game 3 on Wednesday seemed to have unlocked something for the Guardians' superstar. In that one, Ramírez went 2-for-4 with a double, a triple and a stolen base. He took over the game with his bat, glove and his legs. Then Ramírez had even more in store for Game 4.
Just like in Game 3, the White Sox took the momentum early on Thursday, taking a 2-0 lead into the fifth inning and running Guardians starter Parker Messick out of the game after just 2 1/3 innings. But once catcher Patrick Bailey cut the lead in half with a solo shot, it was time for Ramírez to make his mark on the game.
"It's contagious to the team, like the way he plays the game, the energy, his at-bat quality," second baseman Travis Bazzana said postgame. "I mean, we saw him [in Game 3] manufacture a run by himself. He got on, stole some bases and then scored. So he can make the impact so fast, but he plays with such intention."
Prior to Ramírez's fifth-inning at-bat, it felt like a big swing was coming. He flew out in his first at-bat before a sharp lineout in his second. But he found the barrel on both, with exit velocities of 98.9 mph and 97.5 mph, respectively.
Ramírez made sure the third ball he put in play wouldn't be caught. The Guardians' third baseman launched a two-run blast to put Cleveland ahead 3-2 and injected some much-needed confidence into the visiting dugout.
While he doesn't typically show a lot of emotion, Ramírez was sure to fire up his dugout before rounding the bases.
"It's a special moment when you have that type of energy from the guys," he said postgame. "I had a particular conversation with Messick before that. I told him, 'I'm going to get this turned around for you,' and I was able to execute it. It was really special."
Said manager Stephen Vogt: "It was José Ramírez being José Ramírez in the playoffs. Bring in a fastball, [Jordan] Hicks with a great fastball, and Josy got to it. To step up, say there he goes again. And a big moment for him, big moment for us, and he doesn't show a lot of emotion, but he was pretty excited tonight."
Although Cleveland's lead didn't hold long, with Chicago scoring two more in the bottom of the fifth, Ramírez for the second straight day galvanized the Guardians' offense. That three-run outburst in the fifth inning was just an appetizer. The entreé was a monster, six-run sixth inning that made it 9-4 and broke the game open.
As part of that six-run sixth, Ramírez added an RBI single, giving him back-to-back multi-hit games. Since that 0-for-6 in the first two games of the ALDS, the Cleveland superstar is 4-for-9 in the second pair of games, with a double, a triple, a home run, a walk, a stolen base, four runs scored and five RBI.
"It just starts with him. Whether he's hot, whether he's cold, just having him in the lineup, it's that presence," DeLauter said. "When he comes out firing, has that energy, has cool, big swings like that — it just rallies us together."
The numbers will tell you that Ramírez has not been at his best for much of 2026 — he had surgery on the hamate bone in his left hand in June, after all — but you wouldn't know it by his confidence. The seven-time All-Star might not be tall, but he walks around like he's a giant. And that confidence can be felt by everyone around him.
For the Guardians to fight back from a 2-0 series deficit while in Chicago and get back to Cleveland for a chance to reach the ALCS, they needed the best version of Ramírez to show up. And with not a moment to spare, it appears that he has rediscovered his elite form.
Now Cleveland has an opportunity to become the first team since the 2017 New York Yankees to win three straight games in a best-of-five series after losing the first two. Heading back home with a superstar who has gotten hot, an offense that's rolling and a White Sox team that's on the ropes, the Guardians appear to have all the momentum.
"It's going to be crazy," Ramírez said of what he expects for Game 5. "It's going to be an incredible energy. For us, it's going to be the same mindset: Try to win the game, and enjoy the environment that's going to be at Progressive [Field]."

New York Yankees impending free-agent first baseman/designated hitter Paul Goldschmidt has expressed a desire to keep playing at age 39 in 2027, according to Gary Phillips of the New York Daily News. It is unclear if the Yankees will make an effort to re-sign the former MVP and seven-time All-Star in the offseason. Goldy had a nice bounce-back campaign in 2026 in his 16th year in the big leagues after he hit just 10 homers and drove in 45 runs in 146 games in 2025 in his first year in pinstripes. In 105 regular-season games across 380 plate appearances this year, Goldschmidt hit .252/.313/.452 with a .765 OPS, 18 home runs, 52 RBI, and 44 runs scored for the Yankees. He went hitless in eight plate appearances with two walks and a run scored in four postseason games for New York this year. Goldschmidt is obviously no longer in his prime and is no longer an everyday player, but he should still attract interest across the league for his ability to hit lefties. In 183 plate appearances against southpaws in 2026, he hit .299 (47-for-157) with 11 of his 18 home runs and 24 RBI.--Keith Hernandez

Steven Kwan is going to have his name floating through trade rumors as soon as the Cleveland Guardians‘ season ends, and until he’s either moved, signs an extension, or the next season begins with him still on the roster.
Really, Kwan has been in the rumors since the middle of the 2025 season. The Guardians rarely keep players beyond their first six years of club control, and with that in mind, they often then trade them away to ensure they get some value rather than losing them in free agency for nothing.
Some rumors are more palatable for Cleveland supporters than others, though.
Because the latest trade idea involving Kwan would send him to the Chicago Cubs — the team that broke Cleveland’s hearts in the 2016 World Series.
Steven Kwan to Cubs?
Bleacher Report’s Kerry Miller included the Guardians trading Kwan to the Cubs as part of his new article on Monday examining “realistic” trades for the offseason.
He puts together the whole package, one that would have the Guardians sending Kwan to the Cubs for two prospects.
The two players Cleveland would get in return in this proposal are right-handed pitcher Jaxon Wiggins and utility man James Triantos. Both are former second-round picks who have yet to debut in the major leagues.
“On the prospects front, Jaxon Wiggins entered 2026 as a top 100 prospect on Baseball America, Baseball Prospectus and MLB, but he was a mess at Triple-A Iowa, walking nearly 20 percent of batters faced,” Miller writes. “Maybe Cleveland can fix his command, though, while James Triantos has .300 batting average, 30 stolen bases potential to replace Kwan.”
As far as player types, those guys both fit the Cleveland mold. The Guardians love to make pitchers better, and they certainly would enjoy a speedy contact guy like Triantos.
Dealing away Kwan would still be a tough pill to swallow for the Cleveland fanbase regardless.
Why Guardians Would Trade Steven Kwan
It all comes down to money in Cleveland.
When players get near the end of their contracts, the choice is either to extend them for more cash, or send them away for future value.
Aside from Jose Ramirez, the Guardians generally choose the latter approach.
“At any rate, two winters ago, they traded away the final five seasons of their seven-year contract with Andrés Giménez, and subsequently shipped Josh Naylor to Arizona, rather than paying what ended up being a $10.9M salary in his final year of arbitration eligibility,” Miller writes. “Despite their penny-pinching ways, they just keep making the postseason, winning the AL Central for the seventh time in 11 years. So, if they can turn one year of Kwan into a pair of former second-round picks, history suggests they probably will.”
Kwan is entering the final year of his contract. He’s arbitration-eligible for the final time and will probably get paid $10-11 million for 2027.
Whether it’s the Guardians paying him that or a different team is what this offseason will determine.

item.content:encoded:
The MLB playoffs are here as 12 teams survived the regular season and are ready for an all-out battle for October supremacy. Each of the remaining squads has spent the last six months proving it belonged in the postseason. None of the last teams standing got here unscathed and all have glaring weaknesses that could end their seasons early.
With postseason baseball upon us, here is the fatal flaw that could derail each MLB playoff team.
Brewers: Lack of Power
The Brewers were baseball’s best team all season but that doesn’t mean they’re perfect. Milwaukee has a great rotation fronted by baseball’s new ace Jacob Misiorowski, and a good bullpen, but the lineup relies heavily on getting hits up and down the lineup. The Brewers play the 2026 version of small ball, and don’t have a ton of power. That can kill teams in October, when runs come at a premium.
Milwaukee finished the season tied for 28th in home runs (154) and 25th in isolated power (.144). The Brewers were tied for 10th in slugging (.403) and were third in wRC+ (107), but the lack of top-line power could be their downfall. Against elite pitching in the postseason, it’s much more difficult to string together hits and build big innings. Being able to get runs on balls that leave the yard is huge. Each of the last six World Series champions ranked inside the top five in regular season home runs.
Maybe Milwaukee bucks that trend, but if they don’t win the World Series, a lack of power may be the reason.
Dodgers: Health
The Dodgers have won two straight titles and at full strength, they’d be the overwhelming favorite to take home a third in a row. But L.A. has dealt with major injuries all season and the team looks more vulnerable than it has in a long time as we enter the postseason.
Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow combined to make only 22 starts this season. Both are back now, but neither has been particularly reliable—Snell left his penultimate start on Sept. 16 with a groin injury before returning to pitch four innings on Saturday. Tarik Skubal had elbow surgery earlier this year with the Tigers and hasn’t been quite as dominant as usual when it comes to limiting baserunners. Shohei Ohtani has been sidelined by knee and biceps injuries, and won’t be pitching in October. Freddie Freeman, Mookie Betts and Teoscar Hernandez are showing signs of decline and have played a ton of baseball over the last three years.
L.A. is still loaded, but a few injuries to a roster that’s had its fair share of medical issues could make things dicey.
Rays: Trouble Against Lefties
It’s hard to find too many flaws here. The Rays are an incredibly balanced squad that was the best in the AL pretty much all season. One of the only red flags here is the team’s performance against lefties, and they’re likely to run into a few in the playoffs.
Against lefties as a team, Tampa Bay ranked 27th in slugging (.364), 26th in wRC+ (90) and 25th in OPS (.679). Luckily for the Rays, their best offensive players hammered lefties. Junior Caminero slashed .287/.426/.490 with eight home runs and a 152 wRC+. Unfortunately, the 23-year-old and Yandy Diaz are the team’s only players who appeared in 100-plus games and topped .700 in OPS against lefties.
That’s a weakness opponents will try to exploit in October. The Rays don’t have many holes, but good left-handed pitching could be the kryptonite that slows one of baseball’s most complete teams.
Braves: A Hole at Shortstop
The Braves have plenty of star power in the lineup and Chris Sale at the top of their rotation but they have a huge flaw at the heart of their team. Atlanta’s shortstops were among the worst offensively during the 2026 season. Ha-seong Kim is is the starter, but he had a .359 OPS with zero home runs in 147 plate appearances this season so I’m not sure that is the answer. The other option is Mauricio Dubón, who had a .719 OPS in 153 games, but that won’t work against southpaws since it means lefty Mike Yastrzemski must play left field.
Collectively, Braves shortstops slashed .241/.295/.349 during the regular season and ranked 27th with a wRC+ of 78. They also ranked 23rd in fWAR (1.6) and bWAR (-0.4). They simply haven’t gotten enough out of the position and need to find some offensive production there.
Atlanta went wire-to-wire to win the NL East and did so while not getting much from a premium position. Against elite pitching in the postseason, they’ll need production out of everyone in the lineup at some point. Carrying an empty spot will likely prove to be more damaging than it already has been.
Yankees: An Aaron Judge-Sized Hole in the Lineup
The Yankees may have baseball’s best postseason rotation and found enough offense to hold onto the AL’s top wild-card spot. But to win a World Series, they need their best player healthy and hammering baseballs. They may not have it.
Aaron Judge is trying to return for the wild-card series from a strained calf muscle, but it would be unwise to rush him back into action. Yes, New York needs his bat in the lineup, but it also needs to ensure he is available for the entire postseason, not just the first series. Ben Rice (149), Cody Bellinger (115) and Paul Goldschmidt (111) are the only Yankees with more than 300 plate appearances and a wRC+ over 100. That’s a scary lack of production from the lineup.
They need Judge’s bat back at full health as soon as possible simply because the team relies on him so much to produce.
Padres: Who Starts After Michael King?
The Padres have baseball’s best bullpen and an offense that has been clicking on all cylinders in the second half. What they don’t have is a deep rotation after injuries have decimated it.
Michael King is the team’s ace and should be reliable in that spot, but after him things get dicey. Nick Pivetta missed most of the season due to a flexor strain in his pitching elbow that cost him nearly five months. He’s back and has thrown well, but he’s only made eight starts this year. After that, it’ll be some combination of Robbie Ray and Walker Buehler. Both have been up and down this season and neither feels like a rock-solid option.
If San Diego can get decent starts and shorten games by getting the bullpen in early, things could be fine. But if the team’s starters struggle it could mean an early exit.
Cubs: A Battered Starting Rotation
The Cubs have one of baseball’s best offenses and its best all-around player in Pete Crow-Armstrong, but their pitching staff remains a patchwork mess. The team’s starting rotation has endured season-ending injuries to Cade Horton and Ben Brown, Justin Steele still hasn’t returned after elbow surgery in 2025, Matthew Boyd missed time thanks to knee surgery and a shoulder issue, and Kevin Gausman is now dealing with a shoulder injury.
Chicago will open the postseason with Boyd on the mound and should follow with Clay Holmes in Game 2, then Shota Imanaga and, if he’s healthy enough, Gausman. How bad has it been for the Cubs? Among starters, only Imanaga generated 2.0 bWAR this year. That’s a dangerous weakness to carry into the postseason when pitching becomes even more important.
Could the Cubs manage to overcome a rotation that has been battered all season? It’s possible, but that would take a herculean effort from the team’s top-ranked offense.
Phillies: Trea Turner’s Disappearing Production
Trea Turner was a key piece of the Phillies’ success in 2025, as he slashed .302/.354/.450 with 15 home runs, 36 stolen bases and a 123 wRC+ in 141 games. The team is probably wondering where that guy went.
In 157 games this year, Turner slashed .242/.297/.378 with 19 home runs, 21 stolen bases and a wRC+ of 83. His strikeout rate jumped from 16.7% to 21.0%, his xBA dropped from .270 to .242 and his xwOBA of .293 ranked in the 14th percentile. That would be manageable if Turner provided value defensively, but his outs above average dropped from 17 in 2025 to -8 this season. That’s a precipitous, ominous drop for a shortstop who’s in his age-33 season, has always depended on his athleticism and still has seven more years on his contract. Philadelphia has underachieved as a whole in 2026, and Turner is the poster child.
While he was a disappointment in the regular season, Turner has a ton of playoff experience and won a title with the Nationals in 2019. Maybe he’ll turn it around when the lights are the brightest. But his postseason track record doesn’t offer much optimism. He has a career playoff OPS of .681.
Red Sox: A Top-Heavy Offense
Boston’s comeback story this season was remarkable after Alex Cora was fired following a 10–17 start. While they were one of MLB’s best teams over the final two-thirds of the season, the offense never really clicked one through nine. As a team, the Red Sox finished 17th in wRC+ (99) and 19th in OPS (.717). And it seemed all season a few guys would come through, while the rest of the lineup struggled.
Among the team’s hitters who played at least 100 games, only Willson Contreras (151), Wilyer Abreu (112) and Ceddanne Rafaela (109) topped 100 in wRC+ to grade out as above-average hitters. The drop-off from Contreras to the rest of the roster is pretty alarming in itself, though Mickey Gasper (130), Masataka Yoshida (108) and Roman Anthony (106) all performed well in fewer than 300 plate appearances. Key pieces like Caleb Durbin (100) and especially Jarren Duran (69) had off years, while catcher Adley Rutschman slashed .222/.278/.410 with a wRC+ of 88 after arriving at the trade deadline.
Boston will have to overcome those issues throughout the lineup, particularly against the kind of pitching ahead in the postseason. The lack of offensive balance could be the team’s downfall.
Guardians: A Lineup Short of Firepower
The Guardians are in an enviable position, as they barely made the playoffs but wound up with the AL’s No. 2 seed. While they are set up for success thanks to the bracket and have an excellent pitching staff, their lineup has been anemic.
Cleveland finished the regular season ranked 27th in home runs (162) and slugging (.380), 26th in OPS (.696), 24th in runs scored (678) and 21st in wRC+ (97). Meanwhile, star third baseman José Ramírez wrapped up the worst full season of his career, slashing .235/.320/.368 with 12 home runs and a wRC+ of 92. The question is simple: Where do the runs come from? Rookie Chase DeLauter was the team’s most productive hitter after slashing .287/.363/.456 with 16 home runs and a 131 wRC+, but he doesn't have much help. Steven Kwan was second on the team in wRC+ (114), but only slugged .349, while Travis Bazzana (110) and Angel Martinez (108) were both only modestly above average by wRC+. The rest of the lineup struggled to generate offense.
After a tough battle down the stretch, the Guardians wound up with a favorable path in the postseason. But getting to the World Series will likely require unearthing some unsung heroes on offense.
White Sox: October Inexperience
The White Sox surprised everyone with their run to a postseason berth after three consecutive 100-loss seasons. The roster has been properly overhauled, with only 19.8% of the team’s plate appearances coming from players on the 121-loss team in 2024. The problem is, most of the team’s new players have little to no postseason experience.
Braden Montgomery, Munetaka Murakami and Sam Antonacci are rookies, while Colson Montgomery, Kyle Teel, Chase Meidroth and Grant Taylor are second-year players. Sean Burke debuted in 2024, but has never pitched in the postseason, and All-Star Miguel Vargas has likewise never appeared in the postseason despite coming up with the Dodgers. Maybe there’s something to be said for youthful exuberance, but there’s also the possibility that fatigue becomes a factor for players who haven’t been through a playoff chase before. Colson Montgomery posted a wRC+ of 54 after August 1, while Murakami slashed .156/.299/.375 in that stretch.
Chicago is built for success long-term, but its lack of postseason experience could be a significant obstacle in October.
Astros: A Thin Starting Rotation
The Astros finished 81–81 to win the weak AL West and notch a playoff spot. Given their record, it’s not surprising they have a ton of issues across the roster. The most glaring is their starting rotation, which is in rough shape.
Beyond Hunter Brown, Houston simply doesn’t have the kind of high-end starting pitching that wins in October. And even Brown enters the playoffs with some uncertainty, having thrown only 107 ⅓ innings this season after missing a chunk of the campaign with a shoulder injury. Peter Lambert has become the team’s No. 2 starter, but he went 8–10 with a 3.82 ERA and doesn’t possess premium stuff. Hayden Wesneski finished the season strong, but made only 11 starts all year, while Cristian Javier and Mike Burrows are both on the IL.
The rotation is so thin that the Astros are poised to open Game 1 of the wild-card series with a bullpen game to give Brown, Lambert and Wesneski rest. It’s hardly an ideal situation and there aren’t many options available for manager Joe Espada.
Ryan Phillips is a senior writer on the Breaking and Trending News team at Sports Illustrated. He has worked in digital media since 2009, spending eight years at The Big Lead before joining SI in 2024. Phillips also co-hosts The Assembly Call Podcast about Indiana Hoosiers basketball and previously worked at Bleacher Report. He is a proud San Diego native and a graduate of Indiana University’s journalism program.

item.content:encoded:
(Commentary)
Here's the thing about all the agita related to the Los Angeles Dodgers, MLB's competitive balance and the 2026 postseason: No outcome this October will change the calculus for the team owners.
Even if the small-market Milwaukee Brewers, Tampa Bay Rays or Cleveland Guardians win the World Series, the league will continue its push for a salary cap, contending the sport lacks sufficient parity and is effectively broken.
Not that long ago, the league was making precisely the opposite argument. Its public-relations department, in news releases before the 2021 and 2022 seasons, described competitive balance as a hallmark of MLB.
Let's be clear: Revenue disparity between large- and small-market clubs is a legitimate concern. The league and players union need to adopt significant measures to make the playing field more level. But the league's argument for greater competitive balance, if not a red herring, is at least an argument of convenience. And not a particularly strong one, if you watched the regular season.
The Brewers finished with the best record in the National League. The Rays produced the best record in the American League. And the Guardians became the third small-market team to earn one of four first-round byes. Perhaps the Guardians were undeserving, considering their record was only the 11th best in the majors. But by finishing with the second-best mark among AL division winners, they clinched the bye under the postseason format the league and union created.
So is the sport really that far gone?
The league's own news release in 2022 noted that MLB produced 15 different World Series champions in the prior 21 seasons. The Texas Rangers in 2023 made it 16. And before the 2024 World Series, MLB Commissioner Rob Manfred told The Athletic, "Our record on competitive balance is darn good."
Just two years later, to hear Manfred & Co. tell it, the sport is having an existential crisis. All because the league's highest-revenue team, the Dodgers, won back-to-back World Series. All because the team owners want to build their case for a cap.
The league cites a need for greater competitive balance as justification to drastically overhaul the game's economic system. And it is trumpeting a new set of facts -- specifically, the absence of a small-market champion since the 2015 Kansas City Royals -- to make its case.
There is no denying that in that time, large-market teams have accounted for 90% of World Series winners, 85% of World Series participants and 77.5% of league championship series participants. And sure, the same pattern might continue this year.
Never mind that the Dodgers performed below expectations in the regular season for the second consecutive year. According to FanGraphs, they still stand the best chance of winning the World Series -- 36.7%, with the Brewers next at 11.6%. As if on cue, and in some cases by design, the Dodgers' best players are getting healthy and rounding into form.
If Los Angeles becomes the first team since the 1998 to 2000 New York Yankees to win three consecutive World Series titles, the league will surely use that data point in its pitch that only a salary cap can save the sport.
And if the Brewers or Rays win their first Series, or if the Guardians win their first since 1948? The league will consider it an aberration, a single-season outcome that means little when compared with the larger sample size of the previous 10 seasons. An exception that proves the rule.
But let's broaden the discussion.
By emphasizing postseason results, the league is devaluing the most accurate measure of a club, the six-month grind of the regular season. Not to mention devaluing the 162 games of inventory all 30 clubs must sell.
Since 2015 -- the line of demarcation the league has set with the Royals' World Series triumph -- the Guardians rank fourth in regular-season wins, the Brewers fifth and the Rays seventh. They are models for other small-market teams, proof that those clubs do not have to operate without hope.
It's true none of those teams won a World Series in the past 10 years. But the Rays got there in the shortened 2020 season. The Guardians reached the American League Championship Series in 2024, the Brewers in 2025. Inferior depth, resulting in part from lower payrolls, might be part of the reason none went further. Adjustments to the collective bargaining agreement could help address that.
No reasonable person would start a league from scratch and adopt baseball's current economic system, in which the league says that the top four spenders -- the Dodgers, New York Mets, Yankees and Philadelphia Phillies -- outspent the bottom 22 in free agency over the course of the current labor agreement.
Reasonable people can disagree, however, whether a cap is the only possible solution when the players' historic opposition to the concept might lead to the cancellation of part or all of the 2027 season.
The league keeps referencing polls saying fans want a cap. Fans, though, evidently are not too upset with the current state of affairs: The league's attendance increased again this year, reaching its highest level since 2016.
Even in cap sports, not every team begins every season with the expectation of competing for a title. The most successful franchises are the shrewdest. Part of baseball's problem is that innovative small-market clubs no longer hold the competitive advantage they once did over less forward-thinking opponents.
Ex // Top Stories
Some of the large-market teams plucked top small-market executives. Very few clubs, if any, continue to lag behind in the intellectual arms race. Even the Colorado Rockies and Washington Nationals, two of the slowest clubs to adapt to baseball's information age, have gotten smarter.
If everyone is essentially working off the same data, payrolls become more of a separator. But even then, the edge money provides is not an absolute guarantee of success in October.
Before winning in the shortened 2020 season, the Dodgers had not won a World Series since 1988. The Mets have not won since 1986. The Phillies and Yankees are experiencing championship droughts that began in 2008 and 2009.
Many baseball executives consider the postseason a crapshoot, fearing the random outcomes that occur in small samples.
The Dodgers, without question, have inordinate financial advantages, including the right to withhold a healthy portion of their massive local TV deal from revenue sharing, a benefit that arose from a settlement the league reached in bankruptcy court with the team's former owner Frank McCourt.
Still, the Dodgers in 2022 and 2023 were eliminated in the division series by rivals from smaller markets, the San Diego Padres and Arizona Diamondbacks. In 2024, the Dodgers' first year with Shohei Ohtani, they nearly lost to the Padres again in division series play. And if not for a series of fortuitous events, they would have lost the 2025 World Series to the Toronto Blue Jays.
Another thing lost in the discussion about the Dodgers' dominance is that villains are good for business. This is the third consecutive season the Dodgers led the majors in road attendance. Their spending forces other NL clubs to try to keep pace. The small-market Padres, in particular, are better for it.
Yet the ability to spend is sometimes a double-edged sword. Long-term contracts sometimes backfire. Seemingly capable of papering over any mistake by simply printing more money, the Dodgers roll merrily along even when free-agent additions such as Kyle Tucker, Edwin Díaz and Tanner Scott slump. But several of the Dodgers' biggest and most expensive stars are facing age-related decline. A number of other top-10 payroll clubs, including the Padres, are locked into the same kinds of players.
None of that means that the league and union should proceed as if all is well, assuming the game's cyclical nature will balance things out. The concerns of the small-market clubs must be addressed, and the union acknowledged as much in May with its initial proposals, some of which addressed revenue disparity.
The union proposed enhanced revenue sharing that included protections "to ensure clubs prioritize winning over profiteering"; financial rewards for successful revenue-sharing recipients and draft-pick incentives for them to sign free agents and retain their own players on the verge of hitting the open market.
The league scoffed at the union proposals, as one might expect with the collective bargaining agreement months away from expiration and the parties holding completely different worldviews. Finding a middle ground will be tricky. At least to this point, large-market clubs are willing to share more revenue -- and yield their inherent financial advantages -- but only under a cap system that fixes their costs.
Teams like the Brewers, Rays and Guardians clearly do not require more money to win regular-season games. But the way they operate, frequently trading stars as they get closer to free agency, is far from fan-friendly. Brewers fans buying a Jacob Misiorowski jersey and Rays fans buying a Junior Caminero jersey know not to get too attached to those players. As one small-market executive says: "Championships are won with talent, continuity and experience. We can get talent. The other two are tough to come by."
Tough, but not impossible. Countless examples exist of revenue-sharing recipients signing homegrown players for the long term. The Brewers did it with Jackson Chourio, Cooper Pratt and Luis Lara, the Guardians with José Ramírez and Tanner Bibee. The Pittsburgh Pirates might not keep Paul Skenes, but they locked up Konnor Griffin. The Royals secured extensions with Bobby Witt Jr. and Maikel Garcia, the Seattle Mariners with Cal Raleigh and Julio Rodríguez, the Arizona Diamondbacks with Corbin Carroll and Geraldo Perdomo.
Based on its proposals, the union thinks giving small-market teams an even better opportunity to retain players would benefit the sport. A salary cap is not necessary to make those adjustments and others to the collective bargaining agreement. Much as the league would like fans to believe otherwise, this is not an all-or-nothing situation.
In June, a reporter asked Manfred why he portrays a league he described in 2024 as having a "darn good" record on competitive balance to be out of whack just two years later.
"In the context, particularly of the postseason, where you're trying to generate interest and maximize viewership, I think it's important to emphasize competitiveness," Manfred said. "And there are aspects of competitiveness."
He added: "When we think about it from a labor perspective, we're focused on an entirely different part of the calendar. And that's the offseason, when you're trying to sell season tickets, and the perception among our fans that's really strong that we have a lack of competitiveness."
Maximizing viewership in the postseason? Viewership in the United States last year was the sport's highest since 2017. Selling season tickets? Sure, it's a problem in markets where team owners do not adequately invest in their franchises. It should be less of a problem in places like Milwaukee, Tampa Bay and Cleveland, if we're just talking about the product.
Make the current system fairer, and those clubs will stand even better chances of reaching a postseason that the league expanded to 12 teams from 10 in 2022. Give those clubs enough cracks at the postseason, and eventually one or more will break through.
It could happen this year, if the Brewers, Rays or Guardians win the World Series. The system needs improvement, no doubt. But if competitive balance is the object, it's a lot closer than it appears.

Back in July, we celebrated the All-Star Game by looking at which participants had the best chance of eventually earning induction into the Hall of Fame. The likes of Bryce Harper, Justin Verlander, and Mike Trout all were locks, and rightfully so.
But as the MLB playoffs prepare to kick off, Verlander and Trout are once again sitting at home. Harper and the Phillies survived a near-collapse to secure a Wild Card seed, and he’s one of many postseason participants who could — and in his case, should — find themselves in the Hall of Fame one day.
Besides the obvious counting stats, what makes a Hall of Famer? As we’ve previously noted, baseball fans have recently accepted 40 bWAR as the standard for a remarkable career. Immaculate Grid is to thank on that front, even if there are players who have cleared that mark but don’t feel like Hall of Famers. Astros shortstop Carlos Correa, who is injured but has a 47.1 bWAR, is a perfect example, and he didn’t crack our list.
Instead, let’s turn our attention to someone who may very well become the second unanimous electee when his time comes.
Honorable mention: The Shohei Ohtani tier
Barring any unprecedented rule changes, Hall of Fame candidates must have 10 full seasons worth of experience for eligibility. That means Shohei Ohtani would technically be ineligible if he retired tomorrow, so he won’t land in the “lock” tier.
But Ohtani has always been a unicorn, so him having his own category makes all too much sense. We can all agree that, at this time next year, Ohtani should be a lock on that list.
Not yet eligible, but…
These guys don’t get their own table, but we wanted to address their situations ahead of the playoffs.
- Aroldis Chapman, P, Boston Red Sox: Off the numbers alone, Chapman and his 402 saves (ninth all-time) likely warrant induction. However, he also served a 30-game suspension in 2016 for violating the league’s domestic violence policy. It’s difficult to envision him earning the 75 percent required for election. Recent voting trends don’t work in favor of those who have been suspended for performance-enhancing drugs (more on that soon) or off-field incidents.
- Cam Schlittler, SP, New York Yankees and Jacob Misirowski, SP, Milwaukee Brewers: We’re lumping these two together because both will be trending during the playoffs. Just because these two are likely to win their league’s respective Cy Young Awards doesn’t mean they’re guaranteed a spot in Cooperstown. Heck, we don’t even know if they’ll pitch long enough to appear on a ballot! But, you know how baseball fans are.
- Fernando Tatis Jr., 2B/RF, San Diego Padres: As things currently stand, Tatis has no chance of getting into the Hall of Fame. Voters have made it clear that those who serve PED-related suspensions, as Tatis did in 2022, aren’t welcome in Cooperstown unless they buy a ticket. That said, we’re including him here
- Tarik Skubal, SP, Los Angeles Dodgers: Skubal became the 23rd pitcher in MLB history to win multiple Cy Young Awards, which will appeal to voters who prefer the "dominant" peak. But we’d like to see at least two or three more years of him being at least above-average. He’s also only seven seasons in, so he has a lot of work left.
On pace to make it into Cooperstown
- Alex Bregman, Chicago Cubs - 48.9 bWAR
- Matt Olson, Atlanta Braves - 44.2 bWAR
- Yordan Alvarez, DH, Houston Astros - 30.5 bWAR
These three have team success, specifically at least one World Series ring, working in their favor. Alvarez is likely to win AL MVP, and the 29-year-old is young enough that clearing 40 bWAR shouldn’t be an issue so long as healthy.
Bregman turns 33 next March, and his bWAR is likely far greater than you’d have guessed. But is he truly on a Hall of Fame trajectory? He's nowhere close to 2,000 hits (1,411) or 300 home runs (237), both of which are vital numbers when playing the hot corner.
Consider, though, that Bregman has averaged 24 home runs, 84 RBIs, 32 doubles, and 4.6 bWAR over the last five years. He’s under contract through 2030, and exceeded all of those numbers (28 home runs, 93 RBIs, 33 doubles, and 5.8 bWAR) this season.
If Bregman were to continue averaging those numbers, he’d end the 2031 season with 333 home runs, roughly 2,200 hits, and 481 doubles. Oh, and his bWAR would be right around 72.0, so we imagine he’d be a first-ballot inductee.
Unfortunately for him and Olson, the possibility of a work stoppage could have a monumental impact on their final counting stats. Which leads us into…
Borderline veterans
- Giancarlo Stanton, New York Yankees - 47.0 bWAR
- Zack Wheeler, Philadelphia Phillies - 46.6 bWAR
- Gerrit Cole, SP, New York Yankees - 45.8 bWAR
- Christian Yelich, Milwaukee Brewers - 45.1 bWAR
- Xander Bogaerts, SS, San Diego Padres - 44.3 bWAR
- Max Fried, P, New York Yankees - 32.3 bWAR
- Kyle Schwarber, OF/DH, Philadelphia Phillies - 22.3 bWAR
Stanton and Schwarber’s cases are likely dependent on whether they surpass 500 home runs. The latter will enter next season at 385 homers, and he turns 34 in March. But the looming work stoppage could significantly affect his chances of reaching 400 anytime soon.
As for Stanton, multiple lower-body injuries limited him to three homers in 24 games. Although he has 466 career home runs, the 2017 NL MVP turns 37 in November and is a free agent after next year.
The only members of the 500-home run club who aren’t in the Hall of Fame are either ineligible or have ties to performance-enhancing drugs. It’d be pretty remarkable if Schwarber and Stanton both cleared the historic total yet fell short of Cooperstown.
Personally, Wheeler and Cole are probably the only ones who will have a legitimate Hall of Fame résumé when they become eligible. The rest of those guys are Hall of Very Good at best. Much like Skubal, we need two or three more elite seasons from Fried before we’d even consider voting for him.
Go ahead and make the Hall of Fame plaque
- Mookie Betts, Los Angeles Dodgers - 79.0 bWAR
- Freddie Freeman, Los Angeles Dodgers - 66.8 bWAR
- Paul Goldschmidt, New York Yankees - 65.1 bWAR
- Aaron Judge, New York Yankees - 64.2 bWAR
- Manny Machado, San Diego Padres - 63.3 bWAR
- Chris Sale, Atlanta Braves - 62.7 bWAR
- José Ramírez, Cleveland Guardians - 60.3 bWAR
- Bryce Harper, Philadelphia Phillies - 56.9 bWAR
- Jose Altuve, Houston Astros - 53.4 bWAR
Outside of Goldschmidt and Sale, none of these names are overly surprising. And no, the Astros’ sign-stealing scandal shouldn’t impact Altuve, especially not after Carlos Beltrán just entered the Hall of Fame.
Goldschmidt currently ranks 143rd on the all-time bWAR list, and only 31 men above him aren’t already enshrined. But of the 20 who are or were eligible, most came up short for PED or off-field reasons. The question then becomes whether he’s wearing a Diamondbacks or Cardinals cap, or if he opts for the blank hat.
Although Sale turns 38 next March, he has a lifetime 2.95 ERA and 2,779 strikeouts, putting him within range of reaching 3,000. There’s absolutely no reason why he shouldn’t be a first-ballot selection.
As for the rest? You know a Hall of Famer when you see one, and they more than meet the expectations.

Field Level Media

28 Sep 2026, 10:25 GMT+10

(Photo credit: Ed Szczepanski)
Rookie Lucas Spence ripped a two-run triple to highlight a four-run third inning, helping the Houston Astros celebrate the American League West title with a 9-0 victory over the Athletics on Sunday in West Sacramento, Calif.
Christian Walker homered to lead off the sixth inning and joined Yainer Diaz, Cam Smith and Jeremy Pena in collecting two hits and an RBI for the Astros (81-81), who won the division for the eighth time in the last 10 seasons.
Third-seeded Houston will host the Chicago White Sox on Tuesday in Game 1 of the best-of-three wild-card series. The Astros went 5-2 against the White Sox this season.
Houston actually captured the AL West title prior to the conclusion of its victory, as the Texas Rangers dropped a 6-4 decision to the Minnesota Twins on Sunday.
Yordan Alvarez went 1-for-4 with an RBI single to boost his batting average to .316, giving him his first batting title.
Lawrence Butler had two of the five hits for the Athletics (64-98), who lost for the ninth time in 12 games.
Phillies 7, Tampa Bay 3
Zack Wheeler pitched six strong innings and Kyle Schwarber drove in two runs as the Phillies clinched their fifth straight postseason berth by beating the Rays.
Bryce Harper and Edmundo Sosa homered for Philadelphia, which had lost its previous four games by the combined score of 23-3. The Phillies finally showed signs of life in Game 162, and now they'll head to Atlanta to face the Braves in the National League wild-card round that begins on Tuesday,
Johnny DeLuca homered twice for Tampa Bay. The Rays earned a bye into the American League Division Series and face the winner of the wild-card series between the New York Yankees and Boston Red Sox.
Cubs 6, Red Sox 2
Alex Bregman went 4-for-4 with two home runs and four RBIs against his former team to help Chicago wrap up the regular season by defeating Boston in St. Petersburg, Fla.
The game was scheduled to be played in Boston, but was moved to Tropicana Field because of the nor'easter that hit much of New England throughout the weekend.
Both of Bregman's home runs came against Boston starter Tanner Houck, who made his first appearance on the mound since May 2025. Houck (0-1), who had Tommy John surgery last year, allowed three runs on four hits in three innings. The Red Sox were held to five hits and were 0-for-7 with runners in scoring position.
Twins 6, Rangers 4
Josh Bell hit a two-run home run and drove in three to lead host Minnesota to a season-ending win over Texas.
The loss eliminated the Rangers from the American League West title race and the playoffs. Rangers starter Mackenzie Gore allowed one hit and one run in 2 1/3 innings.
Twins starter Dean Kremer (5-5) gave up three hits and one run in seven innings. Kremer yielded a home run to Danny Jansen, but did not allow another Texas runner past first base.
Dodgers 5, Giants 1 (10 innings)
Andy Pages capped a four-run 10th inning with a three-run home run, and visiting Los Angeles beat San Francisco to earn its 100th win of the season.
The Dodgers took the lead in the 10th when Alex Call's two-out double off the left field fence drove in automatic runner Miguel Rojas. The Giants then elected to walk Max Muncy, before Pages foiled that strategy by driving a pitch by Duncan Davitt (0-1) into the left field bleachers for his 23rd home run of the season.
Alex Vesia (3-1), whose perfect ninth sent the game into the 10th, was credited with the win, which allows the Dodgers to take a three-game winning streak into their National League Division Series opener next Saturday against the winner of the wild-card series between the host Atlanta Braves and Philadelphia Phillies.
Marlins 5, Braves 3
Heriberto Hernandez and Griffin Conine slugged solo home runs, giving host Miami a win over Atlanta to end its season on a high note.
Marlins ace Sandy Alcantara tossed a scoreless ninth inning for his third career save. It was a fitting end of the year for Alcantara, who threw both the first and last pitch of the season for Miami. sStarter Janson Junk left with a no-decision. He allowed three hits and one run in 4 2/3 innings. Michael Petersen (4-4) earned the win with 1 1/3 hitless innings of relief.
Braves starter JR Ritchie (1-5) took the loss. He allowed seven hits and four runs in 5 2/3 innings. Mauricio Dubon hit his 12th homer to open the scoring and added an RBI single for Atlanta, which begins its home wild-card series against divisional rival Philadelphia on Tuesday.
Nationals 6, Mets 4
Andres Chaparro had three hits, including two solo home runs, and host Washington beat New York to end its season with a series win.
Will Dion (3-2) pitched two scoreless innings for the victory and Erik Tolman worked the ninth for his fifth save for Washington, which improved by 11 wins over 2025.
Francisco Lindor hit his 300th career homer and Ronny Mauricio smacked his third home run in two games for the Mets, who finished last in the National League East. Carson Benge ended his rookie season with three hits and an RBI.
Blue Jays 5, Reds 1
In potentially his final career start, Max Scherzer struck out seven over seven-plus innings and host Toronto topped Cincinnati.
The 42-year-old Scherzer (4-9) allowed one run and six hits to earn his 225th career win and boost his strikeout total to 3,557. The Blue Jays' 37-year-old designated hitter George Springer, who might have also played his last game, like Scherzer received a standing ovation when he was replaced.
Brandon Valenzuela hit a two-run home run for Toronto and Charles McAdoo added a solo shot in the rubber match of the three-game series. Brandon Williamson (5-5) allowed four runs and four hits in three innings for the Reds.
White Sox 4, Rockies 2
Randal Grichuk and Brenton Doyle smacked two-run home runs and Anthony Kay pitched five strong innings to boost host Chicago past Colorado.
The White Sox are set to visit the American League West champion Houston Astros on Tuesday in the opener of an AL wild-card series. Chicago clinched its first playoff berth on Thursday since 2021 but was eliminated from contention for an AL Central title with Saturday's loss to Colorado and a Cleveland victory at Kansas City.
Cole Carrigg homered for Colorado, which finished with more than 100 losses for the fourth successive season.
Royals 3, Guardians 2
Vinnie Pasquantino's second solo homer of the day broke an eighth-inning tie and sent host Kansas City to a win over Cleveland.
Jac Caglianone and Kyle Isbel each had two hits for the Royals, who ended a disappointing 2026 campaign by avoiding a sweep and winning for just the seventh time in the final 25 games.
Daniel Schneemann and Jo Adell each homered and had two hits apiece for the Guardians, who rested key regulars Steven Kwan, Jose Ramirez and Brayan Rocchio one day after securing their third consecutive American League Central title. Cleveland plays either the Chicago White Sox or Houston Astros in the American League Division Series.
Pirates 4, Tigers 2
Jared Jones pitched four innings of one-hit ball and Konnor Griffin led off the game with a solo home run and drove in two runs to lead Pittsburgh past host Detroit.
Griffin's homer was the sixth of his rookie season and helped the Pirates secure their first winning record since 2018 and only their second since last making the postseason in 2015. Jones was not eligible for the win after exiting the game before the fifth. Jones finished 5-6 with a 3.72 ERA in 21 starts after returning from elbow surgery in late May.
Rookie River Ryan (0-1) made his second start for the Tigers and sixth of his career. The right-hander allowed two runs on three hits over 1 1/3 innings. Detroit finished with a losing record after advancing to the American League Division Series each of the past two seasons.
Padres 9, Diamondbacks 4
Gavin Sheets homered and Freddy Fermin knocked in three runs as host San Diego tuned up for their National League wild-card series by stopping visiting Arizona.
San Diego, which opens its best-of-three series Tuesday night against the visiting Chicago Cubs, snapped a 4-4 tie with three runs in the bottom of the seventh. Fermin capped it with a two-run single.
Michael Soroka pitched 4 2/3 innings for Arizona, which was eliminated from postseason contention when Philadelphia beat Tampa Bay around the same time San Diego's Jake Cronenworth drew a bases-loaded walk to push home the go-ahead run in the seventh.
Brewers 6, Cardinals 4
Jacob Misiorowski strengthened his case for the National League Cy Young Award, allowing just two hits over five-plus scoreless innings, as host Milwaukee beat St. Louis to close with five consecutive wins and its franchise record for victories in a season (103).
Misiorowski (16-5) allowed two singles in 5 1/3 innings and lowered his major league-leading ERA to 1.80. The right-hander struck out five, giving him 252 strikeouts for the year.
Cardinals starter Andre Pallante (12-9) allowed six runs on 10 hits in five innings. He allowed six singles in the first inning for a 3-0 Brewers lead as well as Gary Sanchez's home run in the third.
Mariners 7, Angels 4
Logan Gilbert pitched four-plus hitless innings and struck out eight as host Seattle dealt Los Angeles its 100th loss of the season. It was also the last game for Dan Wilson as the Mariners' manager. The team announced after the game that Wilson will not return in that role in 2027 after a disappointing season and third-place finish in the American League West.
Jose Siri homered for the Angels, losers of 100 games for the first time. They had been the lone active MLB team to never suffer that many defeats.
Gilbert didn't allow a baserunner until walking Moises Ballesteros leading off the fifth. He struck out the side in the first inning to reach 200 strikeouts for the season, becoming the fourth pitcher in franchise history to do so in multiple seasons.
--Field Level Media
